blocks.h: 1. What OPRC is, and the casualty that produced it

blocks.p: The International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation, 1990 was adopted on 30 November 1990 and entered into force on 13 May 1995. It was developed in the aftermath of the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989, which demonstrated that even a well-resourced State could be overwhelmed by a major spill, and that there was no international framework for asking anyone else for help.

It is a framework convention. It sets no discharge standard and prescribes no construction requirement. Instead it obliges its Parties to build and maintain a capability — plans, authorities, equipment, exercises — and to make that capability available to each other. Its architecture was extended to chemicals by the OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000.

blocks.h: 2. Purpose and objectives - and what OPRC deliberately is not

blocks.p: The objectives are the three nouns in the title:

ol: Preparedness — that plans, designated authorities, pre-positioned equipment, trained people and rehearsed procedures exist before the incident, not after it;
Response — that a State can act promptly and effectively against an oil pollution incident, through a known chain of command and known contact points; and
Co-operation — that States assist one another, and that the legal and administrative friction which delays cross-border assistance is removed in advance.

blocks.p: Three supporting objectives serve those: reporting, so that an incident becomes known at once; information exchange and research and development, so that response technique improves; and technical co-operation, so that developing countries can build the same capability.
It is worth as many marks to say what OPRC is not:

ul: It is not a prevention convention. Preventing pollution — discharge limits, oil filtering equipment, segregated ballast, double hulls — is MARPOL’s work. OPRC begins where prevention has already failed.
It is not a liability or compensation convention. Who pays, and how much, is the CLC, FUND and Bunkers regime. OPRC allocates no liability and creates no fund.
It creates no direct duty on a shipowner. It binds States, which is why the duty that reaches the ship arrives through MARPOL.

blocks.h: 3. The architecture - what the Convention obliges Parties to build

blocks.p: The substantive articles can be held as a sequence — plan, report, react, build, share:

ul: Article 3 — oil pollution emergency plans. Each Party requires ships flying its flag to carry an oil pollution emergency plan in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization, and imposes parallel requirements on offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities under its jurisdiction.
Article 4 — oil pollution reporting procedures. Masters and persons in charge report without delay any event involving a discharge or probable discharge of oil, to the nearest coastal State.
Article 5 — action on receiving a report. The Party assesses the incident and notifies all States whose interests may be affected, together with the Organization.

Article 6 — national and regional systems. The core building obligation. Each Party establishes a national system for responding promptly and effectively, including a national contingency plan, a designated competent national authority and an operational contact point; and, within its capabilities, a minimum level of pre-positioned response equipment, a programme of exercises and training, and detailed plans and communications capability.
Article 7 — international co-operation in response. Parties agree to co-operate and provide advisory services, technical support and equipment on request, subject to their capabilities and resources.
Articles 8 to 10 — research and development, technical co-operation with developing countries, and the promotion of bilateral and multilateral agreements, from which the regional arrangements grow.
Article 12 — the institutional role, placing information services, education and training, and technical services with IMO.

blocks.h: 4. The responsibilities of the flag State

blocks.p: A Party wears two hats under OPRC and the question asks about only one. Separate the flag State’s duties from the same State’s coastal State duties — conflating them is the commonest structural error in this answer. As flag State, its responsibilities are:

ol: Require the plan. Under article 3, require ships entitled to fly its flag to have on board an oil pollution emergency plan, as required by and in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization.
Approve the plan. Through MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.1, the plan must be approved by the Administration — so this is not a document the ship simply writes for itself.
Require reporting. Under article 4, require masters and persons having charge of its ships to report without delay to the nearest coastal State.

Ensure the plan is usable. Under regulation 37.2, ensure it is based on the Organization’s guidelines and written in the working language of the master and officers — an emergency plan in a language the crew does not read is worthless.
Survey, inspect and enforce. Verify at statutory survey that the plan exists, is approved and is current; and take enforcement action against its own ships for breach.
Train and exercise. Ensure crews are drilled on the plan — discharged in practice through the ISM Code and the ship’s safety management system.
Co-operate and communicate. Respond to requests for information about its ships, support the coastal State that receives a report, and maintain the contact arrangements that make that possible.
Implement domestically. Give the Convention force in national law — in India, at this sitting, through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it.

blocks.p: What is not a flag State duty: the national contingency plan, the pre-positioned equipment stockpile and the national response organisation under article 6 are owed by the State in its territorial and coastal capacity, not because it registers ships. Saying so expressly shows the distinction has been understood rather than missed.

blocks.h: 5. The documents required to be carried on board

blocks.p: The operative document is the Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP). OPRC article 3 requires the Party to require it; the detail — thresholds, approval, language and contents — is supplied by MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.

Regulation 37.1: every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above, and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 gross tonnage and above, shall carry on board a shipboard oil pollution emergency plan approved by the Administration. Note that the two thresholds are different, and that the tanker threshold is the lower.

Regulation 37.2: the plan shall be prepared based on guidelines developed by the Organization and written in the working language of the master and officers, and shall consist “at least” of four things — so the list is a floor, not a ceiling:

rows: The procedure to be followed by the master or other persons having charge of the ship to report an oil pollution incident, as required in article 8 and Protocol I of MARPOL, based on the Organization’s guidelines
The list of authorities or persons to be contacted in the event of an oil pollution incident
A detailed description of the action to be taken immediately by persons on board to reduce or control the discharge of oil following the incident
The procedures and point of contact on the ship for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities in combating the pollution

blocks.p: Regulation 37.3 — the combination rule. Where regulation 17 of MARPOL Annex II also applies to the ship, the SOPEP may be combined with the shipboard marine pollution emergency plan for noxious liquid substances; and in that case the title of the combined plan shall be “Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan” — the SMPEP. This is why a chemical tanker carries an SMPEP and not a SOPEP, and it is a favourite oral question.

Regulation 37.4 adds a requirement that is easy to overlook: all oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more shall have prompt access to computerized, shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs — the emergency response service the master calls after a grounding or collision.

Found alongside the plan, but properly labelled as belonging to other instruments rather than to OPRC: the Oil Record Book Part I (and Part II for tankers) under Annex I regulation 17; the IOPP Certificate and its Supplement; and the coastal State contact list which is kept current as part of the plan itself.

blocks.h: 6. How OPRC and MARPOL interlock

blocks.p: The closing point is the one that shows the two instruments have been read together. OPRC binds States; MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the ship. Article 3 requires the Party to require the plan “as required by and in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization” — and those provisions are regulation 37, which supplies the thresholds, the approval requirement, the language rule and the four contents. A single document in the wheelhouse therefore discharges an obligation created in one convention and specified in another, and it is enforced through MARPOL’s machinery — verified at statutory survey, and checked by a port State control officer.

Set beside its neighbours the division of labour is clean: MARPOL prevents, OPRC prepares and responds, and CLC, FUND and Bunkers compensate. Three instruments, one incident, three entirely different questions. Above all of them UNCLOS article 199 obliges States to develop and promote contingency plans for responding to pollution incidents, and OPRC is how that obligation was given operational content.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints 16 marks in one block with no sub-division, and it hides the seam between its first two tasks behind a comma splice — “...Convention, Discuss the responsibilities...”. That is a printed anomaly, it is reproduced rather than corrected, and the practical consequence is that a candidate must supply the structure the paper does not: three tasks, and the word “Briefly” governs only the first.

So the purpose and objectives get two short sections and no more. The flag State duties and the documents are where the marks are, and each gets a substantial one. The four mandatory SOPEP contents go in a table, because that is a four-item list an examiner will scan for and either find instantly or not find at all.

The closing section on how OPRC and MARPOL interlock is not decoration. It is the single highest-value paragraph in the answer, because it demonstrates that the candidate knows why the third task is answered out of a different instrument from the one the question names.

blocks.h: The structural fact that most answers miss

blocks.p: OPRC binds States. It does not bind ships.

Article 3 does not say “every ship shall carry a plan”. It says each Party shall require ships flying its flag to have one, in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization. Those provisions are MARPOL Annex I regulation 37, which is where the 150 GT and 400 GT thresholds, the approval by the Administration, the working language rule and the four contents all live.

This matters for two reasons. It explains why the answer to “list the documents required to be carried on board as per its provisions” is drawn from MARPOL. And it explains enforcement: a port State control officer who wants to check the SOPEP does so under MARPOL’s machinery, because OPRC gives no one power over a ship.

blocks.h: Three conventions, one incident, three questions

blocks.p: The clearest way to hold the whole subject:

rows: How do we stop it happening?
Is anyone ready, and can they help each other?
Before and during — plans, authorities, equipment, response

blocks.p: A candidate who writes a paragraph about double hulls, or about limitation of liability, has answered a different question and will be marked accordingly. Stating the boundaries expressly is itself worth marks in a “discuss the purpose and objectives” task.

blocks.h: Flag State or coastal State? Keep the two hats apart

blocks.p: This is the discriminating feature of the second task. The same State does both, but the question asks about one:

ul: As flag State — require the plan, approve it, require reporting, make the plan usable in the crew’s language, survey and enforce, train and exercise, co-operate, and implement domestically.

As coastal State — the article 6 national contingency plan, the competent national authority and operational contact point, the pre-positioned equipment, the exercise programme, and the article 5 duty to assess a report and notify affected States and IMO.

blocks.p: A candidate who lists the national contingency plan as a flag State responsibility has misread the Convention. Saying explicitly “these are owed in the territorial capacity, not as flag State” converts a possible error into a demonstrated distinction.

blocks.h: The SOPEP details that get dropped

ul: Two different thresholds. 150 GT for oil tankers; 400 GT for ships other than oil tankers. Candidates routinely give one figure for both.
Approved by the Administration. Not written by the master, not issued by class in its own right.
Working language of the master and officers. An explicit requirement of regulation 37.2, and a common oral question.
“At least”. The four contents are a minimum. Company plans are routinely longer and that is compliant, not excessive.
The combination rule. Combined with the Annex II regulation 17 plan, the document is retitled “Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan”. That is why chemical tankers carry an SMPEP.

Regulation 37.4. Oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more must have prompt access to computerized shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs. Almost nobody mentions it and it is a whole limb of the regulation.
The Oil Record Book is not an OPRC document. If it is mentioned, label it as Annex I regulation 17.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing OPRC as a pollution prevention convention. It is preparedness, response and co-operation.
Bringing liability, limitation or compensation into it. That is CLC, FUND and Bunkers.
Saying OPRC directly requires ships to carry a SOPEP. It requires Parties to require it; MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 imposes it on the ship.
Giving one tonnage threshold for both tankers and other ships.
Listing the national contingency plan and equipment stockpile as flag State duties.
Omitting the approval requirement, or the working-language requirement.
Treating the four contents as exhaustive when regulation 37.2 says at least.
Calling a combined plan a SOPEP after combination — it is retitled SMPEP.
Listing the Oil Record Book, IOPP Certificate and Garbage Management Plan as OPRC documents without labelling their real source.
Missing regulation 37.4 entirely.
Writing at length on the purpose when the paper says “Briefly”, and then running short on the two substantial tasks.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: “When was OPRC adopted and when did it enter into force?” Adopted 30 November 1990; in force 13 May 1995.
“Which casualty led to it?” The Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989.
“Does OPRC prevent pollution?” No — it assumes the spill has happened. Prevention is MARPOL.
“Your ship is 380 GT and not a tanker. Does it need a SOPEP?” No — regulation 37.1 catches other ships at 400 GT and above. A 380 GT oil tanker would, because the tanker threshold is 150 GT.
“Who approves the SOPEP?” The Administration.
“What language must it be in?” The working language of the master and officers.
“Name the four things the plan must contain.” Reporting procedure; contact list; immediate action description; and shipboard co-ordination procedures and point of contact.
“Your chemical tanker carries a combined plan. What is it called?” A Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan — regulation 37.3 fixes the title.

“What extra does a 30,000 dwt tanker need under regulation 37?” Prompt access to computerized shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs — the 5,000 dwt threshold at 37.4.

“Whom does the master report to after a spill?” Under OPRC article 4, without delay to the nearest coastal State; the procedure itself is in the SOPEP under regulation 37.2.1, referring to MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What do the letters OPRC stand for? Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation.

Name three things article 6 requires a national system to have. A national contingency plan; a competent national authority and operational contact point; a minimum level of pre-positioned response equipment, with exercises and training.
Which article requires the emergency plan? Article 3.
Which article requires reporting, and to whom? Article 4 - without delay, to the nearest coastal State.
Which Protocol extends OPRC to chemicals? The OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000.
Which MARPOL regulation actually requires the SOPEP? Annex I regulation 37.
What is India's national system called in outline? A national oil spill disaster contingency plan with a designated response authority - the shape article 6 requires.
Which UNCLOS article obliges contingency planning? Article 199.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Start from the title, because the title is the objectives: PREPAREDNESS, RESPONSE, CO-OPERATION. Then add the negative in one line: not prevention, not compensation.
For the architecture, five verbs in article order: PLAN (3), REPORT (4), REACT (5), BUILD (6), SHARE (7 to 10).
For the flag State, four verbs: REQUIRE, APPROVE, VERIFY, ENFORCE — and one caution: the contingency plan is the coastal hat, not the flag hat.

For the SOPEP, two numbers and four contents: 150 and 400; and REPORT, CONTACT, ACT, CO-ORDINATE — which is also the order in which the plan is used in a real incident. Then one extra number: 5,000 dwt for shore-based damage stability access.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: OPRC 1990 — adopted 30 November 1990, in force 13 May 1995. Unamended.

Article 3 — oil pollution emergency plans for ships, offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities. Article 4 — reporting without delay to the nearest coastal State. Article 5 — assess and notify affected States and the Organization.

Article 6 — national and regional systems: national contingency plan, competent national authority and operational contact point, minimum pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training. Article 7 — co-operation on request. Articles 8 to 10 — R&D, technical co-operation, bilateral and multilateral agreements. Article 12 — IMO's institutional role.
OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000 — the same architecture for hazardous and noxious substances.

MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 — the shipboard duty. 37.1 thresholds and approval; 37.2 guidelines, working language and the four contents; 37.3 combination with the Annex II plan and the SMPEP title; 37.4 shore-based damage stability access for tankers of 5,000 dwt and above.
MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I — the reporting obligation regulation 37.2.1 cross-refers to. Annex I regulation 17 — the Oil Record Book. Annex II regulation 17 — the NLS emergency plan.
UNCLOS article 199 — contingency plans against pollution; article 194 — the general duty.
India at this sitting: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and rules made under it.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of the evidence

blocks.p: The evidence for this answer splits unusually cleanly, and the split is declared rather than hidden.

The third task is primary. MARPOL Annex I as revised is held in the True Source corpus with a full extractable text layer — resolution MEPC.117(52), adopted 15 October 2004, in force 1 January 2007 — and regulation 37 was read directly from it in full. The thresholds, the approval requirement, the language rule, the four contents, the combination rule and the 5,000 dwt provision are all taken from that text.

The OPRC Convention itself is not held. That is not an oversight of this session: it is an acquisition gap already recorded in the corpus’s own question-mapping records and in its completion report, where OPRC is named as part of a legal and casualty package that has not been built. The Convention’s dates and its article-by-article content are therefore carried at authoritative-secondary level. No article of OPRC is quoted verbatim anywhere in this answer, and no article is attributed a sub-paragraph, because that precision cannot be sourced from a held text.

No Party count is given, and no response equipment specification, stockpile quantity or tier-response threshold is quoted. Tiered response classification is industry practice rather than a Convention requirement.

The Indian national system is described in outline only — the shape an article 6 system takes, and the statute in force at the sitting — because no Indian contingency-plan instrument and no DG Shipping circular is held by the corpus.

Currency. OPRC is unamended and regulation 37 is unamended at this sitting. questions.understand_first: The single most useful thing to hold about OPRC is what it deliberately is not. It is not a prevention convention — that is MARPOL. It is not a liability or compensation convention — that is CLC, FUND and Bunkers. OPRC assumes the spill has already happened and asks a different question: is anybody ready, and can they work together? Its three nouns are in its title — Preparedness, Response, Co-operation — and every article serves one of them. The second useful thing is structural, and it is where most answers go wrong: OPRC binds States, not ships. It tells a Party to require its ships to carry an emergency plan; the duty that actually reaches the vessel, with thresholds, contents and an approval requirement, is MARPOL Annex I. So the third task in this question is answered out of MARPOL even though the question is about OPRC — and saying so is the best single sentence available here.

steps.title: What OPRC is, and the casualty that produced it
points: the International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation, 1990
adopted 30 November 1990, entered into force 13 May 1995
developed after the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989 exposed the absence of any international framework for co-ordinated response
the premise is that no single State or operator has the resources to answer a major spill alone
it is a framework convention - it obliges Parties to build capability, rather than setting a discharge standard
extended to hazardous and noxious substances by the OPRC-HNS Protocol, 2000

steps.title: Purpose and objectives - and what OPRC deliberately is not
points: the three objectives are the three nouns of the title - preparedness, response, co-operation
PREPAREDNESS - plans, designated authorities, pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training, in place before the incident
RESPONSE - a system that can act promptly and effectively, with a known chain of command and contact points
CO-OPERATION - mutual assistance between States, and the removal of the legal and administrative friction that delays it
the supporting objectives - reporting so that a spill is known about at once, information exchange, research and development, and technical assistance to developing countries
IT IS NOT A PREVENTION CONVENTION - MARPOL sets the discharge and construction standards
IT IS NOT A LIABILITY OR COMPENSATION CONVENTION - CLC, FUND and Bunkers do that work
saying what it is not is worth as much as saying what it is

steps.title: The architecture - what the Convention obliges Parties to build
points: article 3 - oil pollution emergency plans, for ships, offshore units, sea ports and oil handling facilities
article 4 - oil pollution reporting procedures, requiring masters and others to report without delay to the nearest coastal State
article 5 - action on receiving a report: assess, and notify affected States and the Organization
article 6 - national and regional systems for preparedness and response, the core building obligation
article 6 requires a national contingency plan, a designated competent national authority and an operational contact point
and a minimum level of pre-positioned response equipment, a programme of exercises and training, and detailed plans and communications capability
article 7 - co-operation in pollution response, assistance on request, subject to capability
articles 8 and 9 - research and development, and technical co-operation with developing countries
article 10 - promotion of bilateral and multilateral agreements, which is where regional arrangements come from
article 12 - the institutional role, placing information services, education, training and technical services with IMO

steps.title: The responsibilities of the flag State
points: separate the flag State's duties from the same State's coastal State duties - conflating them is the commonest error here

REQUIRE THE PLAN - article 3 obliges the Party to require ships flying its flag to have on board an oil pollution emergency plan as required by and in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization
APPROVE THE PLAN - the approval requirement comes through MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.1, the plan being approved by the Administration
REQUIRE REPORTING - article 4 obliges the Party to require masters and persons in charge of ships flying its flag to report without delay
ENSURE THE PLAN IS USABLE - regulation 37.2 requires it to be in the working language of the master and officers, and based on Organization guidelines
SURVEY, INSPECT AND ENFORCE - verify the plan exists, is approved and is current, through the statutory survey regime and through action on its own ships
TRAIN AND EXERCISE - ensure crews are drilled on the plan, which for the flag State is discharged through the ISM Code and the SMS
COOPERATE AND COMMUNICATE - respond to requests for information, and support the coastal State receiving a report from one of its ships
IMPLEMENT DOMESTICALLY - give the Convention force in national law; in India at this sitting through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and rules made under it

NOTE WHAT IS NOT A FLAG DUTY - the national contingency plan, the pre-positioned equipment and the response organisation under article 6 are owed by the State in its territorial capacity, not as flag State

steps.title: The documents required to be carried on board
points: the operative document is the SHIPBOARD OIL POLLUTION EMERGENCY PLAN, and its detail comes from MARPOL Annex I regulation 37
regulation 37.1 - every oil tanker of 150 GT and above, and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 GT and above
the plan must be APPROVED BY THE ADMINISTRATION
regulation 37.2 - prepared on guidelines developed by the Organization, and written in the working language of the master and officers
the plan shall consist AT LEAST of four things - so the list is a floor, not a ceiling
37.2.1 - the procedure for the master or other person in charge to report an oil pollution incident, as required by article 8 and Protocol I of MARPOL
37.2.2 - the list of authorities or persons to be contacted
37.2.3 - a detailed description of the action to be taken immediately by persons on board to reduce or control the discharge
37.2.4 - the procedures and point of contact on the ship for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities
regulation 37.3 - where Annex II regulation 17 also applies, the plan may be COMBINED, and the combined plan is titled 'Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan'
regulation 37.4 - all oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more shall have prompt access to computerized shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs
supporting documents that are NOT OPRC documents but are found with the plan - the Oil Record Book under Annex I regulation 17, the IOPP Certificate, and the coastal State contact list

steps.title: How OPRC and MARPOL interlock
points: OPRC binds STATES; MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 binds the SHIP
OPRC article 3 says the Party shall require the plan 'as required by and in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization'
those provisions are MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 - which supplies the thresholds, the approval, the language rule and the contents
so a single sheet of paper on the bridge satisfies an obligation created in one convention and specified in another
the enforcement also comes from MARPOL's machinery - the SOPEP is verified at survey and checked at port State control
MARPOL prevents, OPRC prepares and responds, CLC and FUND compensate - three instruments, one incident, three different questions
the OPRC-HNS Protocol 2000 repeats the same architecture for hazardous and noxious substances
UNCLOS article 199 sits above both, obliging States to develop contingency plans against pollution

questions.memory_cue: The title is the answer: PREPAREDNESS, RESPONSE, CO-OPERATION (2). Then two structural facts — OPRC binds States, MARPOL binds ships (6) — and the document is the SOPEP, 150 and 400, four contents (5).

quick_revision.recall_15s: OPRC 1990 — adopted 30 November 1990, in force 13 May 1995, after the Exxon Valdez. Objectives are its three title words: preparedness, response, co-operation. It is not prevention (MARPOL) and not liability (CLC/FUND/Bunkers). Architecture: art 3 emergency plans (ships, offshore units, ports, oil handling facilities); art 4 report without delay to the nearest coastal State; art 5 assess and notify affected States and IMO; art 6 national system — contingency plan, competent national authority and operational contact point, pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training; art 7 co-operate on request; arts 8–10 R&D, technical co-operation, bilateral agreements; art 12 IMO. Flag State: require the plan, approve it, require reporting, ensure the working language, survey and enforce, train, co-operate, implement domestically — the national contingency plan is the coastal hat, not the flag hat. Documents: the SOPEP, under MARPOL Annex I reg 37 — oil tankers 150 GT and above, other ships 400 GT and above, approved by the Administration, on IMO guidelines, in the working language of master and officers, containing at least the reporting procedure, contact list, immediate actions and shipboard co-ordination point. Combined with the Annex II plan it is retitled SMPEP (37.3); tankers of 5,000 dwt and above need prompt access to shore-based damage stability programs (37.4). OPRC binds States; regulation 37 binds the ship.
critical_numbers: OPRC adopted 30 November 1990; entered into force 13 May 1995
SOPEP threshold: oil tankers of 150 gross tonnage and above
SOPEP threshold: ships other than oil tankers of 400 gross tonnage and above
MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.2 lists FOUR mandatory contents, and says 'at least'
Regulation 37.4 - oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more need prompt access to shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength programs
OPRC-HNS Protocol adopted 2000
The relevant MARPOL cross-reference for reporting is article 8 and Protocol I
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37 is the provision that actually reaches the ship. Regulation 37.1 requires every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above and every other ship of 400 gross tonnage and above to carry a shipboard oil pollution emergency plan approved by the Administration; 37.2 requires it to be based on the Organization's guidelines, written in the working language of the master and officers, and to consist at least of the reporting procedure, the contact list, the description of immediate action and the shipboard co-ordination procedures and point of contact.
quick_revision.major_trap: Believing that OPRC itself requires the ship to carry a SOPEP. OPRC binds States, not ships: article 3 obliges each Party to require ships flying its flag to have a plan “in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization”, and those provisions are MARPOL Annex I regulation 37, which supplies the two different thresholds, the approval requirement, the working-language rule and the four contents. The paired trap is answering the question as though OPRC were about preventing pollution or about who pays for it — prevention is MARPOL and compensation is the CLC, FUND and Bunkers regime.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State OPRC's full title, its dates, and its three objectives.
retrieval_cards.answer: The International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Co-operation, 1990. Adopted 30 November 1990; entered into force 13 May 1995, developed after the Exxon Valdez grounding of 1989. Its three objectives are the three nouns of its title: preparedness - plans, authorities, equipment and training in place beforehand; response - the ability to act promptly and effectively; and co-operation - mutual assistance between States with the friction removed in advance.
retrieval_cards.why: The title carries the objectives, which makes this the cheapest structured mark on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is OPRC deliberately NOT about?
retrieval_cards.answer: It is not a prevention convention - discharge standards, equipment and construction are MARPOL's work, and OPRC begins where prevention has failed. It is not a liability or compensation convention - that is CLC, FUND and Bunkers. And it creates no direct duty on a shipowner, because it binds States.
retrieval_cards.why: Stating the boundaries is worth as many marks as stating the content, and it prevents a whole paragraph of wrong material.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does OPRC require ships to carry a SOPEP?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not directly. OPRC article 3 requires each Party to REQUIRE ships flying its flag to have an oil pollution emergency plan 'as required by and in accordance with provisions adopted by the Organization'. Those provisions are MARPOL Annex I regulation 37, which supplies the thresholds, the approval requirement, the language rule and the contents. OPRC binds States; regulation 37 binds the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the structural fact the whole question turns on, and it explains why the document limb is answered out of MARPOL.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the SOPEP tonnage thresholds and say who approves the plan.
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex I regulation 37.1: every oil tanker of 150 gross tonnage and above, and every ship other than an oil tanker of 400 gross tonnage and above. The plan must be approved by the Administration. The two thresholds are different and the tanker threshold is the lower.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely give a single figure for both, which loses the mark outright.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the four mandatory contents of a SOPEP.
retrieval_cards.answer: Under regulation 37.2, and the plan shall consist AT LEAST of: the procedure for the master or other person in charge to report an oil pollution incident, as required by MARPOL article 8 and Protocol I; the list of authorities or persons to be contacted; a detailed description of the action to be taken immediately by persons on board to reduce or control the discharge; and the procedures and point of contact on the ship for co-ordinating shipboard action with national and local authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Report, contact, act, co-ordinate - and that is also the order the plan is used in during a real incident.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a SOPEP be based on, and what language must it be in?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 37.2: prepared based on guidelines developed by the Organization, and written in the working language of the master and officers. An emergency plan the crew cannot read is worthless, which is why the language requirement is express.
retrieval_cards.why: A standard oral question, and the language rule is frequently omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A chemical tanker carries one combined pollution emergency plan. What is it called and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan (SMPEP). Regulation 37.3 permits the SOPEP to be combined with the shipboard marine pollution emergency plan for noxious liquid substances required by MARPOL Annex II regulation 17, and provides that the title of the combined plan shall be 'Shipboard marine pollution emergency plan'.
retrieval_cards.why: The retitling is expressly in the regulation and explains why chemical tankers do not carry a document called a SOPEP.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does regulation 37.4 require, and of which ships?
retrieval_cards.answer: All oil tankers of 5,000 tons deadweight or more shall have prompt access to computerized, shore-based damage stability and residual structural strength calculation programs - the emergency response service the master calls after a grounding or collision.
retrieval_cards.why: It is a whole paragraph of the regulation that almost every candidate omits.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which OPRC duties belong to the flag State, and which to the coastal State?
retrieval_cards.answer: Flag State: require the plan (art 3), require reporting without delay (art 4), approve the plan and enforce the working-language and content requirements through MARPOL reg 37, survey and enforce, train and exercise through the ISM system, co-operate, and implement domestically. Coastal State: the article 6 national system - national contingency plan, competent national authority and operational contact point, pre-positioned equipment, exercises and training - and the article 5 duty to assess a report and notify affected States and IMO.
retrieval_cards.why: Listing the national contingency plan as a flag State duty is the commonest structural error in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does OPRC article 6 require a Party to establish?
retrieval_cards.answer: A national system for responding promptly and effectively to oil pollution incidents, including as a minimum a national contingency plan, a designated competent national authority and an operational contact point; and, within its capabilities, a minimum level of pre-positioned oil spill response equipment, a programme of exercises and training, and detailed plans and communication capabilities for responding.
retrieval_cards.why: Article 6 is the core building obligation and is where the Convention becomes a national institution rather than a treaty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: MARPOL, OPRC, CLC and FUND all touch the same oil spill. What does each answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL asks how we stop it happening - construction, equipment and discharge standards, before the event. OPRC asks whether anyone is ready and whether they can help each other - plans, authorities, equipment and response, before and during. CLC, FUND and Bunkers ask who pays - liability and compensation, afterwards. Above all of them UNCLOS article 199 obliges States to develop contingency plans against pollution.
retrieval_cards.why: Three instruments, one incident, three different questions - it keeps prevention and compensation material out of an OPRC answer.

blocks.h: (a) Scope and application of Admiralty Law in India, and the key provisions of the 2017 Act — 8 marks
1. What admiralty law is, and what the 2017 Act was enacted to cure

blocks.p: Admiralty law is the body of law governing maritime claims and, distinctively, the right to proceed in rem — against the vessel itself rather than only against a person. That is what gives it its force: a ship is a valuable and mobile asset, and arresting it produces real security against a defendant who may be a single-ship company incorporated where no judgment could be enforced.

Until 2017 India exercised that jurisdiction under colonial legislation. Section 17(1) of the Act repeals, in their application to India, the Admiralty Court Act, 1840, the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890 and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act, 1891, together with the Letters Patent, 1865 so far as it applied to the admiralty jurisdiction of the Bombay, Calcutta and Madras High Courts.

The Act’s own long title states its purpose: “to consolidate the laws relating to admiralty jurisdiction, legal proceedings in connection with vessels, their arrest, detention, sale and other matters connected therewith or incidental thereto”. It is Act No. 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017, and by section 12 the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 applies to proceedings under it so far as not inconsistent with the Act or its rules.

blocks.h: 2. Scope, application and the jurisdiction of the High Courts

blocks.p: Section 1(2) sets the reach, and it is deliberately wide: the Act applies to every vessel, irrespective of the place of residence or domicile of the owner. A foreign-owned, foreign-flagged ship lying in an Indian port is squarely within it. Two provisos carve out:

ul: an inland vessel as defined in the Inland Vessels Act, 1917, and a vessel under construction that has not been launched, unless notified by the Central Government; and
warships, naval auxiliaries and other vessels owned or operated by the Central or a State Government used for non-commercial purposes, together with notified foreign non-commercial vessels.

blocks.p: “Vessel” is defined broadly at section 2(1)(l) — including barges, lighters, hovercraft, offshore industry mobile units and vessels that have sunk or are stranded or abandoned — but the Explanation removes a vessel broken up to such an extent that it cannot be put into use for navigation, as certified by a surveyor.

Section 3 is the jurisdiction provision. Subject to sections 4 and 5, jurisdiction in respect of all maritime claims vests in the respective High Courts and is exercisable over the waters up to and including the territorial waters of their respective jurisdictions. The proviso allows the Central Government, by notification, to extend that limit up to the limit defined in section 2 of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976. So the jurisdiction is High Court jurisdiction, and it is territorial with a statutory power of extension.

Two procedural provisions complete the picture: by section 14 an appeal lies from any judgment, decree or final or interim order of a single Judge of the High Court to a Division Bench of that Court; and by section 15 the Supreme Court may transfer an admiralty proceeding from one High Court to another. Section 2(2) imports the meanings of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 for words not defined in this Act.

blocks.h: 3. Maritime claims, arrest in rem, liens and priority

blocks.p: Section 4(1) recognises twenty-three heads of maritime claim, (a) to (w). They are best grouped:

rows: Possession and ownership; co-owner disputes over employment or earnings; mortgage or charge; sale contract disputes; insurance premium including mutual insurance calls; commission, brokerage and agency fees
Loss or damage caused by the operation of a vessel; loss of life or personal injury, on land or water, in direct connection with that operation; loss of or damage to goods

Carriage of goods or passengers; use or hire; salvage including special compensation; towage; pilotage; supplies, provisions, bunker fuel, equipment and services to the vessel; construction, repair, conversion and equipping; port, harbour, canal, dock and light dues; disbursements
Wages and sums due as wages, cost of repatriation and social insurance contributions — expressly notwithstanding sections 150 and 151 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

Particular and general average (Marine Insurance Act, 1963 meanings); environmental damage and the cost of prevention and restoration; wreck raising, removal and rendering harmless; and maritime lien itself

blocks.p: Section 5 supplies the teeth. The High Court may order arrest of a vessel within its jurisdiction to provide security against a maritime claim where the person or demise charterer liable when the claim arose still holds that position when the arrest is effected; or the claim rests on a mortgage or charge; or relates to ownership or possession; or is secured by a maritime lien under section 9. Under section 5(2) a sister ship may be arrested in lieu — but the proviso bars that for an ownership or possession claim under section 4(1)(a).

Section 9 identifies five maritime liens, and gives them their order among themselves: (a) crew wages and related sums including repatriation and social insurance; (b) loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel; (c) salvage reward including special compensation; (d) port, canal, waterway and pilotage and other statutory dues; and (e) tort claims from loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than to cargo and containers carried on board. A maritime lien continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag — which is what makes it formidable — and is extinguished after one year, or two years for wages, unless arrest or seizure has led to a forced sale. Section 9(4) excludes liens for oil or hazardous and noxious substance damage compensable under other law, and for radioactive properties.

Section 10 then ranks everything in three tiers: first, claims where there is a maritime lien; second, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; third, all other claims. Claims within a tier rank equally, and salvage claims rank in inverse order of time. Finally, section 8 provides that on a judicial sale the vessel vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges; and section 11 protects the shipowner by empowering the court to require the arresting claimant to give an unconditional undertaking or security against a wrongful or unjustified arrest or excessive security demanded.

blocks.h: (b) Assessors in Admiralty proceedings — qualifications, role, and technical assistance to the court — 8 marks
4. Who assessors are, and how they are appointed

blocks.p: The whole statutory basis is section 13, and it is only two sub-sections long.

Section 13(1): “Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the Central Government shall appoint by notification, a list of assessors with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, the nature of duties to be performed by them, the fees to be paid to them and other ancillary or incidental matters for the purposes of this Act, in the manner as may be prescribed.”
Three features of that sentence carry the marks:

ol: the duty is on the Central Government, not on the court or the parties;
the instrument is a notification; and
what is appointed is a list — a standing panel, settled in advance, from which the court draws. Assessors are not selected ad hoc by the litigants.

blocks.p: The same notification fixes their qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, the nature of their duties, their fees, and ancillary matters — all “as may be prescribed”, and section 16(2)(a) gives the Central Government the corresponding rule-making power.

Section 13(2) is short and decisive: “The appointment of assessors shall not be construed as a bar to the examination of expert witnesses by any of the parties in any admiralty proceeding.” That single sub-section fixes the assessor’s constitutional position:

rows: The Central Government, to a list, by notification
The party who calls them, by evidence to the court

blocks.h: 5. Qualifications, role, and how assessors assist the court

blocks.p: Qualifications. The Act itself does not enumerate them; it requires them to be prescribed, and they live in the rules. In substance what is required is professional maritime competence backed by experience — the people appointed are master mariners and chief engineers, naval architects, marine surveyors, salvage and casualty specialists, and marine insurance and admiralty practitioners, with practical experience of the subject matter in issue and the independence to advise a court rather than a client. For a Marine Engineer Officer, Class I, this is a realistic later professional role: the qualification the Act contemplates is precisely a senior engineer’s experience of machinery, survey and shipboard practice.

Role. An assessor exists because a judge is an expert in law and not in ships. Their function is to supply the technical understanding that allows the court to apply the law to facts it can actually follow — and to do so from a position of neutrality, which no party’s expert occupies.
How they assist in interpreting technical maritime matters — concretely:

ol: Translating the evidence. Survey reports, class records, engine performance data, planned maintenance printouts, VDR data and casualty reports are unintelligible to a lay reader. The assessor makes them intelligible and explains the vocabulary.

Establishing what good practice required. Questions of negligence, seaworthiness and due diligence turn on what a competent owner, master or engineer should have done in the circumstances. That is a technical standard, and the assessor explains it.

Testing competing expert evidence. Where two party-appointed experts disagree, the assessor helps the court identify where they actually differ and which assumptions drive the difference — the single most valuable thing an assessor does, and the best protection against a court being persuaded by confident but wrong evidence.

Assessing reasonableness and quantum. Whether a repair specification and its cost were reasonable, whether a salvage effort was proportionate, whether an off-hire period was justified, whether machinery damage was fair wear or a casualty.

Casualty reconstruction. In collision, grounding, fire and machinery-failure cases — manoeuvring characteristics, stopping distances, watchkeeping practice, the sequence of alarms and the plausibility of a claimed failure mode.
Condition and maintenance questions. Where seaworthiness, a repair claim or a crew wages claim depends on the actual state of the ship, its class status and its maintenance history.

blocks.p: The limits matter as much as the role. The assessor does not give evidence and is not cross-examined; the assessor does not decide — the court remains the tribunal of both fact and law; and by section 13(2) the parties retain their full right to call their own experts. The result the Act is aiming at is faster and better-informed adjudication of technical maritime disputes by courts that would otherwise be wholly dependent on the parties for their understanding of the ship.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The printed split is 8 + 8, but the two limbs are not equally heavy in reading. Limb (a) names three separate statutory objects — key provisions, High Court jurisdiction, and the types of maritime claim recognised — and each has to be answered. Limb (b) has three demands too, but the Act gives it only two short sub-sections, so the marks there come from quality of explanation rather than from quantity of citation.

The twenty-three heads of section 4 go in a grouped table. Reciting (a) to (w) in prose is unreadable and wastes the page; five groups with the letters beside them shows the same knowledge in a quarter of the space and proves the candidate has read the section rather than memorised a list.
The assessor/expert-witness distinction goes in a second small table because it is a four-way comparison and because it is the highest-value single idea in limb (b).

blocks.h: What the 2017 Act actually changed

blocks.p: A candidate who says only “the Act governs admiralty jurisdiction in India” has not answered “scope and application”. The examinable point is what it replaced.

Until 2017 Indian admiralty jurisdiction rested on four colonial statutes and a set of Letters Patent — the Admiralty Court Acts of 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891, and the Letters Patent, 1865 for Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. Section 17(1) repeals all of them. The consequences are worth stating: the jurisdiction is now statutory and modern; it is exercisable by the High Courts generally rather than resting on the historic charters of three presidency towns; and the list of maritime claims is now enacted rather than inferred from Victorian case law.

blocks.h: Jurisdiction: which court, how far

blocks.p: Two facts, and both are commonly got wrong.

Which court: the High Courts — section 3 vests it in “the respective High Courts”. Not the district courts, not a specialist tribunal, and not the Supreme Court at first instance (though section 15 lets the Supreme Court transfer between High Courts).

How far: up to and including the territorial waters of the respective jurisdiction — not the EEZ as of right. The proviso to section 3 allows the Central Government by notification to extend the limit to the limit in section 2 of the Maritime Zones Act, 1976. Saying “territorial waters, extendable by notification” is precise; saying “Indian waters” is not.

blocks.h: Maritime claim, maritime lien, mortgage - three different things

blocks.p: This is the distinction that separates a good answer from a competent one, and section 4(1)(w) is the trap: “maritime lien” is itself listed as one of the twenty-three heads of maritime claim. So all maritime liens are maritime claims; almost no maritime claims are maritime liens.

rows: Founds jurisdiction; may support arrest under section 5
Follows the ship through change of owner, registration or flag; first in priority; extinguished after one year (two for wages)
Second in priority — behind every maritime lien

blocks.p: Two consequences follow that examiners like. A financier’s registered mortgage ranks behind the crew’s unpaid wages, which is a deliberate policy choice. And under section 8 a judicial sale wipes the slate clean — the purchaser takes free of all encumbrances and liens — which is why a court-ordered sale, and not a private one, is what makes an arrested ship saleable at all.

blocks.h: Arrest is powerful, and it is not free

blocks.p: Candidates describe arrest as though it were costless leverage. Section 11 says otherwise: the High Court may, as a condition of arrest or of maintaining one, require the claimant to give an unconditional undertaking to pay damages or provide security for loss suffered by the defendant where the arrest was wrongful or unjustified or where excessive security was demanded. That is a real risk to an over-eager claimant.

The other limit is the sister-ship proviso. Section 5(2) allows another vessel to be arrested in lieu — but not where the claim is an ownership or possession claim under section 4(1)(a). The logic is obvious once seen: you cannot claim to own this ship and arrest a different one instead.

And section 11(3) has a practical provision worth knowing: if the owner or demise charterer abandons the vessel after arrest, the court shall auction it within forty-five days, extendable by thirty days for reasons recorded in writing.

blocks.h: Limb (b): the assessor is not an expert witness

blocks.p: Everything in limb (b) hangs off section 13(2). The appointment of assessors is not a bar to the examination of expert witnesses by any of the parties — so the two coexist, and they are different creatures.

An expert witness is retained by a party, gives evidence, and is cross-examined. An assessor is appointed by the Central Government to a list, advises the court, gives no evidence and is not cross-examined, and does not decide. The assessor is the court’s technical conscience; the expert is an advocate’s technical case.

Note also the mechanism: a list, appointed in advance by notification. That is a deliberate design choice — it means neutrality and availability are settled before any particular dispute arises, rather than being fought over inside it.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Saying admiralty jurisdiction lies in any civil court. Section 3 vests it in the High Courts.
Saying the jurisdiction extends to the EEZ as of right. It runs to territorial waters, extendable only by Central Government notification.
Confusing maritime claim with maritime lien. Twenty-three claims, five liens — and maritime lien is itself head (w).
Putting the registered mortgage first in priority. Section 10 puts maritime liens first, mortgages second.
Saying a maritime lien survives a judicial sale. Section 8 vests the vessel free of all liens and encumbrances.
Saying a maritime lien is lost on a change of flag or owner. Section 9(2) says it continues.
Omitting the limitation periods — one year, two years for wages.
Saying any sister ship can always be arrested. Not for an ownership or possession claim — the proviso to section 5(2).
Treating arrest as risk-free. Section 11 exposes the claimant to an undertaking or security for wrongful arrest.
Calling assessors expert witnesses, or saying they give evidence, or saying they decide the case. Section 13(2) and the nature of the office say otherwise.
Saying the court or the parties appoint assessors. The Central Government appoints a list by notification.
Importing the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. It commenced 15 March 2026, almost a year after this sitting. The 1958 Act governs, and it is the Act to which sections 2(2) and 4(1)(o) refer.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: “Give the full name and number of the Act.” The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 — Act No. 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017.
“How many maritime claims does section 4 recognise?” Twenty-three, (a) to (w).
“How many maritime liens are there?” Five — section 9(1)(a) to (e), in that order of priority.
“Crew wages or the bank’s mortgage — who is paid first?” Crew wages. Maritime liens rank ahead of registered mortgages under section 10, and wages head the lien list.

“The ship is sold by the owner to a new owner under a new flag. Is your lien gone?” No — section 9(2), it continues notwithstanding change of ownership, registration or flag. But it dies after one year unless arrest has led to a forced sale.
“The court sells the ship. Is your lien gone?” Yes — section 8, the purchaser takes free of all liens and encumbrances.
“Can you arrest a warship for unpaid bunkers?” No — the second proviso to section 1(2) excludes warships, naval auxiliaries and non-commercial Government vessels.
“Your claim is that you own the ship. Can you arrest her sister instead?” No — the proviso to section 5(2) bars sister-ship arrest for a section 4(1)(a) claim.
“Who appoints assessors?” The Central Government, by notification, as a list — section 13(1).
“Can the parties still call their own experts?” Yes — section 13(2) says the appointment of assessors is no bar to it.
“Does an assessor decide the case?” No. They advise the court; the court decides.
“Where does an appeal go?” Section 14 — from a single Judge to a Division Bench of the same High Court.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which court exercises admiralty jurisdiction in India, and how far out? The High Courts, over waters up to and including territorial waters, extendable by Central Government notification.

What did the 2017 Act repeal? The Admiralty Court Acts 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891, and the Letters Patent 1865 in its admiralty application.
Name five maritime claims. Any five of section 4(1) - e.g. bunkers supplied, crew wages, salvage, towage, environmental damage.
Name the five maritime liens in order. Wages; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; port, canal and pilotage dues; tort damage other than to cargo carried.
How long does a maritime lien last? One year, or two years for wages, unless arrest has led to a forced sale.
State the section 10 priority. Maritime liens; then registered mortgages and charges; then all other claims.
Which section covers assessors, and what does it require? Section 13 - the Central Government appoints a list by notification, with prescribed qualifications, duties and fees.
Are assessors witnesses? No. They advise the court and are not cross-examined; section 13(2) preserves the parties' right to call experts.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: For limb (a), hold the Act as five questions in order, which is also the order of its sections: WHICH COURT (3) → FOR WHAT (4) → WITH WHAT TEETH (5) → WHOSE CLAIM FOLLOWS THE SHIP (9) → WHO IS PAID FIRST (10).

For the five maritime liens, work from the person outwards: CREW → CASUALTY → SALVOR → STATE → STRANGER. Wages, then injury and death, then salvage, then port and pilotage dues, then tort damage to a third party.
For the numbers: 23 claims, 5 liens, 3 priority tiers, 1 year (2 for wages), 45 days (+30) for an abandoned ship’s auction.

For limb (b), one section and one sentence: section 13 — the Central Government appoints a LIST; and 13(2) — that is no bar to expert witnesses. Then the role in four words: TRANSLATE, STANDARD, TEST, QUANTIFY.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 — Act No. 22 of 2017, 9 August 2017. Long title: to consolidate the laws relating to admiralty jurisdiction, proceedings in connection with vessels, their arrest, detention and sale.

s.1(2) — applies to every vessel irrespective of the owner’s residence or domicile; provisos exclude inland vessels, unlaunched newbuildings, warships, naval auxiliaries and non-commercial Government vessels. s.2(1)(l) — wide definition of vessel; broken-up vessels excluded. s.2(2) — undefined words take Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 meanings.
s.3 — jurisdiction vests in the High Courts, over waters up to and including territorial waters; extendable by Central Government notification to the Maritime Zones Act, 1976 limit.

s.4(1)(a) to (w) — twenty-three heads of maritime claim; Explanation imports Marine Insurance Act, 1963 ss.64(1) and 66(2) for particular and general average. s.4(2) to (4) — accounts, sale, title to proceeds, and the arrested vessel as security.
s.5 — arrest in rem; s.5(2) and proviso — sister-ship arrest, barred for s.4(1)(a) claims. ss.6 and 7 — in personam jurisdiction and its restrictions.

s.9 — five maritime liens and their inter se order; continuation through change of ownership, registration or flag; one year, two years for wages; exclusions for oil/HNS and radioactive claims.

s.11 — protection against wrongful or unjustified arrest and excessive security; abandoned vessel auctioned within 45 days, extendable by 30.
s.12 — Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 applies. s.14 — appeal to a Division Bench. s.15 — Supreme Court transfer.

s.13(1) — the Central Government appoints by notification a list of assessors with prescribed qualifications and experience, duties and fees. s.13(2) — no bar to expert witnesses. s.16(2)(a) — the rule-making power over those matters.
s.17(1) — repeal of the Admiralty Court Acts 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Acts 1890 and 1891, and the Letters Patent 1865 in its admiralty application.

Surrounding statutes at this sitting: Merchant Shipping Act, 1958; Marine Insurance Act, 1963; Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976; Inland Vessels Act, 1917; Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, currency and the statute boundary

blocks.p: The statutory content of this answer is primary throughout. The Admiralty Act 2017 is held in the True Source corpus as an official India Code text with construction status complete-official, and every section cited above was read directly from it. There is no evidence gap in the law of this question.

The one genuine gap is the subordinate legislation. Section 13(1) requires assessors’ qualifications, duties and fees to be “prescribed”, and section 16(2)(a) gives the rule-making power — but the rules are not held, and no appointing notification is held. The answer therefore states what the Act provides, and describes the qualifications an assessor would hold as a matter of substance, expressly flagged as not a quotation from any prescribed rule. No fee scale is given.

No decided case is cited. Indian admiralty case law is outside the corpus, and attributing a proposition to a judgment that cannot be checked would be exactly the false precision the production protocol forbids. The stem asks for the Act’s key provisions, and the held text supplies them.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two eight-mark limbs, both legal, and the examiner has made limb (a) markedly more specific than the same family's earlier sittings by NAMING the statute and demanding three particular things from it - key provisions, High Court jurisdiction, and the types of maritime claim recognised. Limb (b) is about assessors and, for a Marine Engineer Officer candidate, is the more interesting half: the assessor is the role an experienced marine engineer might one day occupy, and the added demand 'how they assist the court in interpreting technical maritime matters' is asking the candidate to explain their own future professional function to a court.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as 8 + 8. Limb (a) contains three named statutory objects and is the heavier reading task; limb (b) contains three demands - who, qualifications, and how they assist - but the material is thinner because the Act devotes two sub-sections to it. The answer therefore gives limb (a) three route steps and limb (b) two, and resists the temptation to pad limb (b) with generalities about expert evidence.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: For (a): that the candidate knows the Act's full name and year, that jurisdiction vests in the HIGH COURTS and is territorial, that section 4 lists the claims and can group them convincingly, and that arrest in rem and the maritime lien priority ladder are the Act's teeth. For (b): section 13 by number, that assessors are appointed BY THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT BY NOTIFICATION as a LIST rather than case by case, that their appointment does not bar expert witnesses, and a credible account of what technical assistance actually consists of.
primary_source_plan: Read the Admiralty Act 2017 in full from the held official India Code text
Take the long title verbatim - it states the Act's purpose better than any paraphrase
Take the application and both provisos from section 1(2), because the exclusions are examinable
Take the jurisdiction rule and its territorial limit from section 3, including the extension proviso
Read all twenty-three heads of section 4(1) and GROUP them rather than reciting them
Take the arrest conditions from section 5(1) and the sister-ship rule and its exception from 5(2)
Take the five maritime liens, their order, the one-year and two-year periods and the two exclusions from section 9
Take the three-tier priority ladder from section 10
Take sections 13(1) and 13(2) VERBATIM - they are the whole statutory basis of limb (b)
Take the rule-making power over assessors from section 16(2)(a) and the appeal route from section 14
Take the repealed colonial enactments from section 17 to explain what the Act cured
Run the statute-regression sweep across all eight surface classes for the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025
Cite no decided case and quote no prescribed qualification or fee - the rules are not held
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW as to this Act, which is unamended and stable. HIGH as to the surrounding statute, which is why the question carries the paper's only HIGH flag: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs at this sitting and was repealed on 15 March 2026 by the 2025 Act. Any donor or editor working from a 2026 object would carry the wrong statute into the two places where the Admiralty Act cross-refers to it - section 2(2) and section 4(1)(o).
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH by nature - this is a wholly Indian question and every proposition is domestic. The risk is not of importing foreign law but of importing LATER Indian law. The controls are the statute-regression sweep and the rule that no proposition is stated without a section number from the held text.
technical_ambiguities: Whether admiralty jurisdiction lies in all courts - it does not; section 3 vests it in the High Courts
Whether the jurisdiction is unlimited at sea - it is not; it runs to and including territorial waters, extendable only by Central Government notification
Whether every maritime claim is a maritime lien - it is not; only the five in section 9(1), and section 4(1)(w) lists maritime lien as merely one head of claim among twenty-three
Whether a maritime lien survives a change of owner or flag - it does, by section 9(2), which is what makes it formidable
Whether a maritime lien survives a judicial sale - it does not; section 8 vests the vessel free from all encumbrances and liens
Whether a sister ship can always be arrested - it cannot; section 5(2)'s proviso bars it for an ownership or possession claim under section 4(1)(a)
Whether arrest is risk-free for the claimant - it is not; section 11 exposes it to an undertaking or security for wrongful or unjustified arrest
Whether assessors are witnesses - they are not; they assist the court, and section 13(2) preserves the parties' right to call expert witnesses
Whether assessors are appointed case by case - the Central Government appoints a LIST by notification, from which the court draws
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Five numbered sections under two printed limb headings. Limb (a): one section on origin and purpose including the repeal of the colonial statutes, one on jurisdiction and application, one on the claims and the arrest machinery with the twenty-three heads GROUPED in a table and the priority ladder set out. Limb (b): one section on who assessors are and how they are appointed, taking section 13 close to the text, and one on qualifications, role and the mechanics of technical assistance - which is where a marine engineer candidate can genuinely outperform.
