questions.understand_first: Admiralty is different from ordinary litigation in one respect that explains everything else: you can sue the ship. In an ordinary claim you sue a person and hope they have assets; in admiralty you proceed in rem against the vessel itself, arrest it, and hold a multi-million-dollar asset as security until you are paid or secured. That is enormous leverage against a defendant who may be a one-ship company registered somewhere you will never reach. The 2017 Act exists because India was exercising this power under colonial statutes inherited from the nineteenth century — law that predated the ships it was being applied to. The Act repeals all of that and puts the jurisdiction on a modern statutory footing: it says which court (the High Courts), how far (territorial waters), for what (twenty-three defined heads of maritime claim), with what teeth (arrest in rem, and a maritime lien that follows the ship through a change of flag), and in what order the money is shared. Limb (b) then asks about the one place where a court admits it cannot do this alone: an assessor — a maritime professional the Central Government has put on a list — sits with the judge and explains what the technical evidence actually means.

steps.title: What admiralty law is, and what the 2017 Act was enacted to cure
points: admiralty law is the body of law governing maritime claims and, distinctively, the right to proceed IN REM against the vessel itself
the leverage is the arrest - a ship is a valuable, mobile asset and holding it produces security where a personal claim would produce nothing
before 2017 Indian admiralty jurisdiction rested on colonial statutes
section 17(1) repeals the Admiralty Court Act 1840, the Admiralty Court Act 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890 and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891
and the Letters Patent, 1865 so far as it applied to the admiralty jurisdiction of the Bombay, Calcutta and Madras High Courts
the long title states the purpose - to CONSOLIDATE the laws relating to admiralty jurisdiction, legal proceedings in connection with vessels, their arrest, detention and sale
Act No. 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017; section 12 applies the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 so far as not inconsistent
so the Act modernises, consolidates and Indianises a jurisdiction that had been running on nineteenth-century English statutes

steps.title: Scope, application and the jurisdiction of the High Courts
points: section 1(2) - the Act applies to EVERY VESSEL, irrespective of the place of residence or domicile of the owner
that is the key to its reach - a foreign-owned, foreign-flagged ship in an Indian port is fully within it
first proviso excludes an inland vessel under the Inland Vessels Act, 1917, and an unlaunched vessel under construction unless notified
second proviso excludes warships, naval auxiliaries and Government vessels used for non-commercial purposes, and notified foreign non-commercial vessels
'vessel' is defined broadly at section 2(1)(l) - including barges, lighters, hovercraft, offshore industry mobile units and sunk, stranded or abandoned vessels
but a vessel broken up so that it cannot be put into use for navigation, as certified by a surveyor, is not a vessel
SECTION 3 - jurisdiction over all maritime claims vests in the RESPECTIVE HIGH COURTS
exercisable over the waters UP TO AND INCLUDING the territorial waters of their respective jurisdictions
proviso - the Central Government may by notification EXTEND that limit to the limit in section 2 of the Maritime Zones Act, 1976
section 2(2) - undefined words take their meaning from the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
appeals lie under section 14 from a single Judge to a DIVISION BENCH of the same High Court; section 15 lets the Supreme Court transfer proceedings between High Courts

steps.title: Maritime claims, arrest in rem, liens and priority
points: SECTION 4(1) lists TWENTY-THREE heads of maritime claim, (a) to (w) - group them rather than reciting them

PROPRIETARY AND FINANCIAL - possession and ownership, co-owner disputes over employment or earnings, mortgage or charge, sale contract disputes, insurance premium including mutual insurance calls, commission and brokerage
OPERATIONAL DAMAGE - loss or damage caused by the operation of a vessel; loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with it; loss or damage to goods

CONTRACTUAL AND SERVICES - carriage of goods or passengers; use or hire; salvage including special compensation; towage; pilotage; supplies, bunkers, equipment and services; construction, repair, conversion and equipping; disbursements; port, canal, dock and light dues
CREW - wages, repatriation costs and social insurance contributions, expressly notwithstanding sections 150 and 151 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

AVERAGE AND ENVIRONMENT - particular and general average, taking the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 meanings; environmental damage and the cost of preventive and restoration measures; wreck raising, removal and rendering harmless
AND MARITIME LIEN ITSELF at 4(1)(w)
SECTION 5 - ARREST IN REM, the enforcement mechanism, to provide security against a maritime claim

available where the owner or demise charterer liable when the claim arose still holds that position at arrest, or the claim is on a mortgage, or relates to ownership or possession, or is secured by a maritime lien
section 5(2) - a SISTER SHIP may be arrested in lieu, but the proviso bars that for an ownership or possession claim under 4(1)(a)

SECTION 9 - FIVE MARITIME LIENS in order: crew wages; loss of life or personal injury; salvage; port, canal, waterway and pilotage dues; and tort damage other than to cargo and containers carried on board
section 9(2) - the lien CONTINUES notwithstanding change of ownership, registration or flag, and is extinguished after ONE YEAR - TWO YEARS for wages - unless arrest has led to a forced sale
section 9(4) - no lien for oil or HNS damage compensable under other law, or for radioactive properties
SECTION 10 - priority in three tiers: maritime liens, then registered mortgages and charges, then all other claims; equal claims rank equally and salvage claims rank in INVERSE order of time
section 8 - on judicial sale the vessel vests in the purchaser FREE from all encumbrances and liens; section 11 protects against wrongful arrest by requiring an undertaking or security

steps.title: Who assessors are, and how they are appointed
points: SECTION 13 is the whole statutory basis and it is short - two sub-sections
section 13(1) - notwithstanding anything in any other law, THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT SHALL APPOINT BY NOTIFICATION A LIST OF ASSESSORS
note three things in that phrase - the duty is on the Central Government, the instrument is a notification, and it is a LIST
so assessors are not chosen ad hoc by the parties or by the judge; the court draws from a panel appointed in advance
the list is appointed with such qualifications and experience IN ADMIRALTY AND MARITIME MATTERS as may be prescribed
the notification also fixes the nature of duties, the fees payable, and other ancillary or incidental matters
section 16(2)(a) gives the Central Government power to make rules on exactly those subjects
SECTION 13(2) - the appointment of assessors SHALL NOT BE CONSTRUED AS A BAR to the examination of expert witnesses by any of the parties
that sub-section is the key to the whole limb - it separates the assessor from the expert witness
an assessor advises the COURT; an expert witness is called by a PARTY and gives evidence that can be cross-examined
the assessor is not a witness, is not a judge, and does not decide - the judgment remains the court's

steps.title: Qualifications, role, and how assessors assist the court
points: the Act does not itself list qualifications - it requires them to be PRESCRIBED, and the rules are the place they live

in substance the qualification is professional maritime competence plus experience: master mariners and chief engineers, naval architects, marine surveyors, salvage and casualty specialists, marine insurance and admiralty practitioners
with sea-going or technical experience of the subject matter, and the independence to advise a court rather than a client
THE ROLE - to supply the technical understanding a judge does not have, so that the law can be applied to facts the court can actually follow
HOW THEY ASSIST, concretely - explain the technical vocabulary and the systems in issue, so that survey reports, class records and engine data become intelligible
explain what good practice required in the circumstances, which is what negligence and seaworthiness questions turn on
help the court test conflicting expert evidence - identify where two experts actually differ, and which assumptions drive the difference
advise on the reasonableness of repair estimates, salvage effort, off-hire periods and the quantum of technical damage
assist on collision and casualty questions - manoeuvring, machinery failure, watchkeeping practice and the sequence of events
advise on maintenance, class survey and machinery condition where seaworthiness or a wages or repair claim is disputed
THE LIMITS - the assessor does not give evidence, is not cross-examined, and does not decide the case
the court remains the tribunal of fact and law, and section 13(2) preserves the parties' right to call their own experts
the practical effect - faster, better-informed adjudication of technical maritime disputes, and less risk of a court being misled by confident but wrong expert evidence
for a Marine Engineer Officer this is a realistic later career - the assessor role is precisely what a Class I engineer's experience qualifies them to do

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is five questions the Act answers: which court, how far, for what, with what teeth, and who gets paid first (steps 1–3). Limb (b) is one section and one distinction: section 13 appoints a list, and 13(2) keeps the assessor apart from the expert witness (steps 4–5).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 — Act 22 of 2017. It consolidates Indian admiralty law and by s.17 repeals the Admiralty Court Acts 1840 and 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Acts 1890 and 1891 and the Letters Patent 1865. s.1(2) applies to every vessel whatever the owner's residence, excluding inland vessels, unlaunched newbuildings, warships and non-commercial Government vessels. s.3 vests jurisdiction in the High Courts, over waters up to and including territorial waters, extendable by Central Government notification. s.4(1) lists 23 heads of maritime claim, (a) to (w) — ownership, mortgage, operational damage, injury, cargo, carriage, hire, salvage, towage, pilotage, supplies and bunkers, repairs, port dues, crew wages, disbursements, average, sale, insurance premium, brokerage, environmental damage, wreck removal and maritime lien. s.5 gives arrest in rem, with sister-ship arrest under 5(2) but not for ownership claims. s.9 gives five maritime liens — wages, death or injury, salvage, port and pilotage dues, tort — which survive change of owner, registration or flag and die after one year (two for wages). s.10 ranks liens, then registered mortgages, then all other claims; s.8 makes a judicial sale clean; s.11 protects against wrongful arrest. Assessors: s.13(1) — the Central Government appoints by notification a LIST with prescribed qualifications, duties and fees; s.13(2) — that is no bar to expert witnesses. They advise the court, give no evidence, are not cross-examined and do not decide.
critical_numbers: Act No. 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017
Section 4(1) recognises 23 heads of maritime claim, (a) to (w)
Section 9(1) creates 5 maritime liens, (a) to (e)
Section 10 sets 3 tiers of priority
A maritime lien is extinguished after 1 year - 2 years for crew wages - unless arrest has led to a forced sale
Section 11(3) - an abandoned arrested vessel is auctioned within 45 days, extendable by 30 days
Jurisdiction runs up to and including territorial waters, extendable by notification
Repealed enactments: 1840, 1861, 1890, 1891 and the Letters Patent 1865
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Section 3 of the Admiralty Act 2017 vests jurisdiction over all maritime claims in the respective High Courts, exercisable over the waters up to and including their territorial waters, with a proviso allowing the Central Government to extend that limit. Section 4(1) recognises twenty-three heads of maritime claim, section 5 authorises arrest in rem to provide security for them, section 9 creates five maritime liens that survive a change of ownership, registration or flag, and section 10 ranks liens ahead of registered mortgages and of all other claims. For assessors, section 13(1) requires the Central Government to appoint by notification a list of assessors with prescribed qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, and section 13(2) provides that their appointment is no bar to the examination of expert witnesses by the parties.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 as the governing merchant shipping statute. It received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026, repealing the 1958 Act by section 324(1) — almost a year after this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 governs, and it matters directly because the Admiralty Act cross-refers to it at section 2(2) and disapplies its sections 150 and 151 at section 4(1)(o). The paired substantive trap is confusing a maritime claim with a maritime lien: there are twenty-three heads of claim in section 4 but only five liens in section 9, and it is the lien — not the claim — that follows the ship through a change of flag and ranks ahead of a registered mortgage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the full name of the Act, its number, and what section 17 repealed.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017 - Act No. 22 of 2017, dated 9 August 2017. Section 17(1) repealed, in their application to India, the Admiralty Court Act 1840, the Admiralty Court Act 1861, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890, the Colonial Courts of Admiralty (India) Act 1891, and the Letters Patent 1865 so far as it applied to the admiralty jurisdiction of the Bombay, Calcutta and Madras High Courts.
retrieval_cards.why: The repeal is what 'scope and application' is really asking about - the Act replaced colonial law with a modern statutory jurisdiction.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which court has admiralty jurisdiction in India, and how far does it extend?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 3: jurisdiction over all maritime claims vests in the respective High Courts, exercisable over the waters up to and including the territorial waters of their respective jurisdictions. The proviso allows the Central Government by notification to extend it to the limit defined in section 2 of the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976.
retrieval_cards.why: High Courts, not district courts; territorial waters, not the EEZ as of right. Both halves are commonly got wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish a maritime claim from a maritime lien, and say why it matters.
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 4(1) recognises twenty-three heads of maritime claim, (a) to (w) - and maritime lien is itself head (w). Section 9(1) creates only five maritime liens: crew wages, loss of life or personal injury, salvage, port and pilotage dues, and tort damage other than to cargo carried. It matters because a lien follows the ship through a change of ownership, registration or flag, and ranks ahead of a registered mortgage under section 10.
retrieval_cards.why: All liens are claims; almost no claims are liens - and the difference decides who gets paid.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five maritime liens in their statutory order.
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 9(1): (a) wages and other sums due to master, officers and crew including repatriation costs and social insurance contributions; (b) loss of life or personal injury in direct connection with the operation of the vessel; (c) salvage reward including special compensation; (d) port, canal and other waterway dues and pilotage dues and other statutory dues; (e) tort claims for loss or damage caused by the operation of the vessel, other than loss or damage to cargo and containers carried on board.
retrieval_cards.why: Crew, casualty, salvor, State, stranger - and the order is the priority.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How long does a maritime lien last, and what survives it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 9(2): it continues notwithstanding any change of ownership, registration or flag, and is extinguished after one year - two years for a wages claim under 9(1)(a) - unless before then the vessel has been arrested or seized and that has led to a forced sale by the High Court. Section 9(3): the period runs continuously, excluding time under arrest or seizure.
retrieval_cards.why: The survival through a change of flag is what makes the lien formidable; the one-year cut-off is what makes speed essential.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the section 10 order of priority.
retrieval_cards.answer: First, claims on the vessel where there is a maritime lien; second, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature; third, all other claims. Claims within a category rank equally, and claims for various salvages rank in inverse order of time as they accrued.
retrieval_cards.why: It puts unpaid crew ahead of the financing bank, which is a deliberate policy choice and a favourite oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a maritime lien survive a judicial sale of the vessel?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Section 8: on sale of a vessel by the High Court in exercise of its admiralty jurisdiction, the vessel vests in the purchaser free from all encumbrances, liens, attachments, registered mortgages and charges of the same nature. That is precisely why a court-ordered sale, rather than a private one, is what makes an arrested ship saleable.
retrieval_cards.why: The lien follows the ship through a private sale and is destroyed by a judicial one - the contrast is the examinable point.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When can a sister ship NOT be arrested, and what risk does an arresting claimant run?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 5(2)'s proviso bars sister-ship arrest where the claim is a dispute regarding possession or ownership under section 4(1)(a) - you cannot claim to own this ship and arrest a different one instead. And under section 11 the court may require the claimant to give an unconditional undertaking or security for loss caused by a wrongful or unjustified arrest, or by excessive security being demanded.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates present arrest as costless leverage; the Act deliberately makes it neither unlimited nor free.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who appoints assessors, by what instrument, and in what form?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 13(1): notwithstanding anything in any other law, the CENTRAL GOVERNMENT shall appoint BY NOTIFICATION a LIST of assessors, with such qualifications and experience in admiralty and maritime matters, nature of duties, fees and ancillary matters as may be prescribed. Section 16(2)(a) gives the corresponding rule-making power.
retrieval_cards.why: Not the court, not the parties, and not case by case - a standing panel settled in advance by notification.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an assessor differ from an expert witness?
retrieval_cards.answer: An assessor is appointed by the Central Government to a list, advises the court, gives no evidence, is not cross-examined and does not decide the case. An expert witness is retained by a party, gives evidence for that party and is cross-examined on it. Section 13(2) provides that the appointment of assessors is not a bar to the examination of expert witnesses by any of the parties, so the two coexist.
retrieval_cards.why: Section 13(2) is the whole constitutional basis of the office and is the highest-value idea in limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an assessor actually assist a court in interpreting technical maritime matters?
retrieval_cards.answer: By translating technical evidence - survey reports, class records, engine data, VDR output - into terms the court can follow; by establishing what good practice required, which is what negligence and seaworthiness turn on; by helping the court identify where two party experts genuinely differ and which assumptions drive the difference; by advising on the reasonableness of repair, salvage and off-hire claims; and by reconstructing casualties in collision, grounding, fire and machinery-failure cases. The assessor advises; the court decides.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the third demand the April stem adds over earlier sittings, and it is where a Class I engineer can genuinely outperform.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which merchant shipping statute governs at an April 2025 sitting, and why does it matter here?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026, repealing the 1958 Act by section 324(1) - well after this sitting. It matters directly because the Admiralty Act cross-refers to the 1958 Act at section 2(2), for words not defined in the Admiralty Act, and at section 4(1)(o), which allows crew wage claims notwithstanding sections 150 and 151 of that Act.
retrieval_cards.why: The paper's only HIGH temporal flag, and the cross-references are where a later-sitting answer would carry the wrong statute in.

blocks.h: 1. Where CII sits in law, and where the scheme has reached

blocks.p: The Carbon Intensity Indicator is regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, introduced by the 2021 revised Annex VI (resolution MEPC.328(76)), which entered into force on 1 November 2022. It is the operational half of the short-term GHG measure; EEXI, regulation 23, is the technical half. EEXI is assessed once against the ship’s design; CII is assessed every year against how the ship is actually run.

It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above in the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1. Under that regulation the ship calculates its attained annual operational CII after the end of calendar year 2023 and after the end of each following calendar year, over 1 January to 31 December, using the fuel oil consumption data collected under regulation 27 — the IMO DCS, running since calendar year 2019. Under regulation 28.2 it reports that value to its Administration within three months of the year end.

The position at this examination is precise, and it is not the position of the scheme’s first year. Calendar years 2023 and 2024 are both complete measured years. Ratings for 2023 have been assigned. The attained CII for 2024 fell due for reporting by 31 March 2025 — in the month immediately before this paper. And the SEEMP guidance has moved on: the current edition is the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, resolution MEPC.395(82), adopted 4 October 2024, which superseded the 2022 guidelines.

blocks.h: 2. The mechanism - attained, required, Z and the reference line

blocks.p: The rating is a comparison, not an absolute measurement. Three quantities are needed.

ul: Attained annual operational CII — what the ship achieved. It is the ratio of the total mass of CO2 emitted, M, to the total transport work undertaken, W, in the calendar year. M is the sum of CO2 from all fuel oil consumed, obtained by multiplying each fuel’s DCS consumption figure by its fuel-mass-to-CO2-mass conversion factor.
Required annual operational CII — the target. Regulation 28.4: Required CII = (1 − Z/100) × CIIR.
CIIR — the reference value for the ship type, taken from the 2019 reference line under the G2 guidelines, resolution MEPC.353(78).

blocks.p: Z is the annual reduction factor, and it is what makes the standard tighten each year. Under the G3 guidelines, resolution MEPC.338(76), table 1, relative to the 2019 line:

The blank rows were filled in by resolution MEPC.400(83), adopted on 11 April 2025 — the same month as this examination. It replaced table 1 in full, but left the 2023 to 2026 rows exactly as they stood and supplied only the previously unspecified figures for 2027 onwards. The factor governing the 2025 reporting year is therefore 9 % regardless of when in April this paper was sat, and nothing in this answer depends on the later figures.
The consequence for a ship is blunt: the same operating pattern earns a worse rating every year, because the target moves and the ship does not.

blocks.h: 3. The rating, and what actually attaches to it

blocks.p: Under regulation 28.6 the attained CII is verified against the required CII to give a rating of A, B, C, D or E — major superior, minor superior, moderate, minor inferior, inferior — determined by the Administration or any organization duly authorized by it. Critically, the middle point of rating level C is the required annual operational CII itself: C is the target, not a pass mark below it.

The G4 guidelines, resolution MEPC.354(78), place the boundaries around that midpoint. Their design intent is a fleet distribution: across a ship-type segment, the middle 30 % of ships fall in C, the upper 20 % and a further 15 % in D and E, and the lower 20 % and a further 15 % in B and A. No numeric boundary value is quoted here — the Annex fixes only the midpoint of C, and the boundaries are ship-type-specific tables in the guidelines.

The teeth are in regulations 28.7 to 28.9. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or rated E in any single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions; the SEEMP is reviewed to incorporate it and submitted for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained CII; and the ship must duly undertake those actions. Regulation 28.10 works the other way, encouraging Administrations, port authorities and other stakeholders to provide incentives to ships rated A or B — hortatory language that creates no entitlement.

At this sitting, no ship can yet have been rated D for three consecutive years. The earliest possible run is 2023, 2024 and 2025, and 2025 is only three months old. So in April 2025 the only live trigger for regulation 28.7 is a single E rating — a precise point that distinguishes an answer written for this paper from one written for a later one.

Note also what the regulation does not do. There is no detention, no fine and no certificate withdrawn for a poor rating, and regulation 28 prints no withdrawal, rejection or sanction of any kind. The pressure is commercial — charterers, financiers and cargo owners read the rating — and administrative, through the SEEMP. Regulation 28.11 requires a review to be completed by 1 January 2026, covering among other things the reinforcement of corrective actions and the revision of the Z and CIIR values; that review had not reported at this sitting.

blocks.h: 4. AER - what it measures and why the regulation uses it

blocks.p: The G1 guidelines, resolution MEPC.352(78), draw the distinction the question is really about. A demand-based CII uses the actual mass or volume of cargo carried. A supply-based CII uses the ship’s capacity as a proxy for cargo. AER — the Annual Efficiency Ratio — is the supply-based CII which uses DWT as the capacity; the variant using GT is cgDIST.
So AER is, in grams of CO<sub>2</sub> per deadweight-tonne-mile:

ul: numerator — total CO2 from all fuel consumed in the calendar year, from DCS data;
denominator — the ship’s capacity × total distance travelled, also from DCS data;

capacity is DWT for bulk carriers, tankers, container ships, gas carriers, LNG carriers, general cargo ships, refrigerated cargo carriers and combination carriers, and GT for cruise passenger ships, ro-ro cargo ships including vehicle carriers, and ro-ro passenger ships.

blocks.p: Its virtue is entirely practical: every input is already reported, already auditable and already comparable. Nothing new has to be measured, and two sister ships can be compared on identical terms.

blocks.h: 5. EEOI, and the critical comparison

blocks.p: EEOI — the Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator — is defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684 and measures CO2 per tonne of cargo actually carried per mile. It is the demand-based metric and it is a truer measure of transport work: a ship that sails full has done more work than one that sails in ballast, and EEOI says so where AER does not.

Its status must be stated exactly. EEOI is not the regulatory metric. G1 applies the section 4 indicators to all ships caught by regulation 28, and lists EEOI at section 5 — with EEPI, cbDIST and clDIST — among indicators encouraged to be additionally used for trial purposes. It is voluntary.
The critical case against AER is real and should be made:

ul: it rewards distance, not cargo. A long ballast leg improves it; three weeks at anchor burning fuel and travelling no distance ruins it;

it is blind to utilisation. Two identical ships, one full and one half empty, score identically on the same fuel over the same distance — so the metric cannot reward the commercially efficient operator;
it penalises short-sea and multi-port trades, where port time and manoeuvring are a large share of consumption and sea distance is small;
it can be gamed at the margin by slow steaming with more ships, which lowers each ship’s AER while the cargo moves no more efficiently overall.

blocks.p: The case for choosing it anyway is equally real. EEOI needs cargo mass data that the DCS does not collect, that is commercially confidential, that an Administration cannot verify as it verifies fuel and distance, and that is not comparable across trades — a car carrier, a container ship and a crude tanker cannot be ranked on tonne-miles. IMO therefore chose the metric that could be audited and enforced over the one that is conceptually correct.

That trade-off — enforceability bought at the cost of validity — is the answer to “critically discuss”, and regulation 28.11’s inclusion of the CIIR and Z values within its own review is IMO’s own acknowledgement that the metric is provisional rather than settled.

blocks.h: 6. Operational measures to improve the rating

blocks.p: Because the metric is fuel over capacity-distance, only two things can be done: burn less, or travel further for it. Operational measures dominate because they are available now and cost little.

ul: Speed and voyage management. Consumption rises far faster than speed, so optimising speed to the required arrival time is the single largest lever. Just-in-time arrival converts waiting at anchor — which burns fuel and adds no distance — into a slower, cheaper passage.
Hull and propeller condition. Planned in-water cleaning and propeller polishing against measured performance, not to a calendar.
Trim and draught optimisation against the ship’s own trim data, and optimum ballast — carry no more than is needed.
Weather routeing to avoid added resistance, and autopilot tuning to cut rudder-induced drag.

Machinery and auxiliary load. Shut down surplus generators, use the shaft generator where fitted, run pumps and fans on variable frequency drives, manage cargo heating and inert gas use, and control accommodation HVAC and lighting.
Reduce port and idle consumption — shore power where available, minimise boiler use, avoid unnecessary main engine running.

blocks.h: 7. Technical, fuel and calculation measures, and where they are administered

blocks.p: Technical retrofit. Low-friction and foul-release hull coatings; propeller retrofit or upgrade and energy saving devices such as ducts, fins and rudder bulbs; engine derating with engine or shaft power limitation; waste heat recovery; air lubrication; and wind assistance. Each must be justified for the specific ship and trade — none is universally worthwhile, and no percentage saving is claimed here for any of them.
Fuel. Because the numerator is CO2 and not fuel mass, switching to a fuel with a lower carbon factor — LNG, methanol or a biofuel blend — reduces attained CII directly for the same energy delivered.

Data and calculation — two legitimate levers that are not fuel savings at all. First, DCS data quality: the attained CII is only as good as the reported fuel and distance, so flowmeter calibration, consistent bunker figures and correct noon-report distances bear directly on the rating. The DCS regime is itself moving — resolution MEPC.385(81) replaces appendix IX and, by its operative paragraph 4, invites Parties to consider early application of the revised data submission from 1 January 2025; the amendments were deemed accepted on 1 February 2025 but do not enter into force until 1 August 2025, so at this sitting the early application is an invitation, not a duty.

Second, the G5 interim guidelines, resolution MEPC.355(78), allow defined voyage adjustments — which deduct fuel and the associated distance for qualifying periods — and correction factors, which adjust the numerator or denominator for cases such as ice conditions and ship-to-ship operations. G5 states the boundary itself: their use should in no way undermine the goal of reducing the carbon intensity of international shipping.

All of it is administered through the SEEMP. Under regulation 26 an affected ship’s SEEMP must carry the calculation methodology, the required CII for the next three years, an implementation plan for achieving it and a procedure for self-evaluation and improvement, and it is subject to verification and company audit. The plan is now developed against the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.395(82). That is where an examiner expects the improvement measures to live — inside a verified plan, not in a loose list.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The question is one unlimbed block of 16 marks setting three tasks — explain CII rating, critically discuss AER and EEOI, and list improvement measures — and the middle one is where the marks actually are. “Critically discuss” is not “describe”: a candidate who defines AER and EEOI and stops has answered half of the highest-value task.

Sections 1 to 3 build the mechanism, and they must come first because the AER discussion is meaningless without knowing that the rating is a comparison against a moving target. Sections 4 and 5 are the critical core. Sections 6 and 7 are the improvement measures, split operational from technical so the answer reads as a plan rather than a shopping list — and the operational half comes first because it is what a ship’s engineer actually controls.
The reduction factors go in a table. Four numbers in prose are lost; four numbers in a table with the current year marked are unmissable.

blocks.h: Where the scheme has reached at THIS sitting - the currency marks

blocks.p: This is the single most valuable thing on the question, because a great deal of published material was written in the scheme’s first year and says something different. At April 2025:

ul: 2023 and 2024 are both complete measured years. The scheme is in its third year, not its first.
Ratings exist. Ships hold a CII rating for calendar year 2023. Saying “no ship has yet been rated” is a first-year statement and is wrong here.
The 2024 attained CII fell due for reporting by 31 March 2025 — in the month immediately before this paper, under the three-month rule in regulation 28.2.
Z is 9 % for 2025. Not 5 %, which was 2023, and not 7 %, which was 2024.
No ship can yet have three consecutive D ratings. The earliest possible run is 2023–2025 and 2025 is incomplete, so the only live trigger for regulation 28.7 is a single E.
The SEEMP guidelines are the 2024 edition, MEPC.395(82) of 4 October 2024, which superseded the 2022 guidelines MEPC.346(78).

blocks.p: Any one of those, stated correctly, marks the answer as anchored to its own sitting.

blocks.h: The instrument adopted during the examination month - and why it changes nothing

blocks.p: MEPC.400(83) was adopted on 11 April 2025 and replaced the G3 reduction-factor table. This paper is an April 2025 paper and no examination day is printed on it, so whether the candidate sat before or after 11 April cannot be known.

It does not matter, and that can be shown rather than assumed. The original G3 table printed 5, 7, 9 and 11 per cent for 2023 to 2026 and left 2027 to 2030 blank, footnoted “to be further strengthened and developed taking into account the review of the short-term measure”. MEPC.400(83) supplied those four blanks — 13.625 %, 16.250 %, 18.875 % and 21.500 % — and left 2023 to 2026 untouched.

So Z = 9 % for 2025 on every day of April 2025. The lesson to carry is general: when a boundary falls inside your sitting month, do not guess the date — find out whether the change reaches the thing you are being asked about. Here it does not.

blocks.h: The one thing that must NOT appear in this answer

blocks.p: The IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved at MEPC 83 — on 11 April 2025, inside this examination month. It is not part of the answer, for three independent reasons.

ul: It was approved, not adopted. It was circulated with a view to adoption at an extraordinary session, and that session adjourned without adopting anything.
On an early-April sitting day it had not even been approved, and the day is unknown — so the answer cannot safely assert even the approval.
It is irrelevant to the question. The stem asks about the CII rating, AER and EEOI, all of which live in regulation 28, which is in force and untouched by it.

blocks.p: The correct formula, if it must be mentioned at all in an oral, is “approved and not adopted” — never “pending entry into force”.

blocks.h: The critical argument, stated cleanly

blocks.p: The examiner’s word is critically. The argument to make is that IMO chose an enforceable metric over a valid one.

EEOI is the better measure of what shipping is for — moving cargo. AER measures how far a hull travelled per tonne of CO2, regardless of whether it carried anything. But EEOI requires cargo mass, which is commercially confidential, is not collected by the DCS, cannot be verified by an Administration, and cannot be compared across ship types. AER’s inputs are already reported, already audited and already comparable. So regulation 28 uses AER and G1 relegates EEOI to trial purposes.

The honest closing point is that regulation 28.11 puts the CIIR and Z values inside the scope of its own review — IMO conceding the metric is provisional. A candidate who says that has genuinely criticised the scheme rather than listed its flaws.

blocks.h: AER and EEOI - one line each

blocks.p: AER — supply-based; capacity is a proxy for cargo; capacity is DWT; every input comes from the DCS; this is the regulatory metric under regulation 28. cgDIST is the same idea with GT, used for cruise passenger, ro-ro cargo and ro-ro passenger ships. EEOI — demand-based; uses actual cargo carried; defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684; voluntary, for trial purposes.
The word to hold on to is proxy. Every strength and every weakness of AER follows from substituting capacity for cargo.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Saying no ship has been rated yet. That was true in early 2024; at this sitting ratings for 2023 exist and 2024 has been reported.
Giving the wrong reduction factor. For 2025 it is 9 %, relative to the 2019 reference line.
Saying a single D rating triggers corrective action. It is D for three consecutive years, or E — and at this sitting a three-year run is not yet arithmetically possible.
Saying a D or E rating leads to detention, a fine or a withdrawn certificate. Regulation 28 prints no sanction at all; the consequence is a corrective action plan in the SEEMP.
Quoting rating boundary values. The Annex fixes only that the middle point of C is the required CII; the boundaries are ship-type-specific guideline tables and no value should be invented.
Treating EEOI as a regulatory requirement. It is voluntary and, in G1, for trial purposes.
Confusing CII with EEXI. EEXI is technical and assessed once on design; CII is operational and assessed every year.
Citing the 2022 SEEMP guidelines. MEPC.395(82) of October 2024 superseded them before this sitting.
Stating MEPC.385(81) as in force. It is accepted but not in force until 1 August 2025; the early DCS application is an invitation.
Bringing in the Net-Zero Framework or GFI. Approved during this month, never adopted, and irrelevant to regulation 28.
Listing improvement measures with invented percentage savings. Quote mechanism, not vendor figures.
Forgetting that data quality and the G5 adjustments are legitimate levers alongside burning less fuel.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: “Where does rating C sit?” Regulation 28.6 — the middle point of rating level C is the required annual operational CII. C is the target itself, not a pass mark.
“What happens to a ship rated D this year?” Nothing. It is D for three consecutive years, or a single E, that triggers regulation 28.7 — and at April 2025 no three-year run is yet possible.
“What is Z this year?” 9 % for 2025. And if asked about 2027: those factors were blank in G3 and were supplied by MEPC.400(83) in April 2025.

“A ship waits three weeks at anchor. What does that do to AER?” It worsens it — fuel burned, no distance travelled, so the numerator grows and the denominator does not. The clearest illustration that AER measures distance, not work.
“How would EEOI treat the same three weeks?” The same way in the numerator, but EEOI at least credits the cargo actually carried on the voyages either side.

“Can an owner improve CII without touching the ship?” Yes — speed and voyage management, better DCS data quality, and the G5 voyage adjustments and correction factors where the ship genuinely qualifies.
“Which guideline gives what?” G1 the indicators and calculation, G2 the reference lines, G3 the reduction factors, G4 the rating boundaries, G5 correction factors and voyage adjustments.
“Who assigns the rating?” The Administration, or any organization duly authorized by it, from the attained CII verified against the required CII.
“Is CII in the SEEMP?” Yes — regulation 26, and the plan is now developed against the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.395(82).

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which regulation is CII, and which Annex? Regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, from MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022.
Which ships? Ships of 5,000 GT and above in the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1.
Write the required CII formula. Required CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference.
What is the reference year for the reference line? 2019.
What is Z for the current year? 9 per cent for 2025.
What is AER in words? Grams of CO2 per deadweight tonne-mile, using capacity as a proxy for cargo.
Where is EEOI defined and what is its status? MEPC.1/Circ.684; voluntary, for trial purposes under G1 section 5.
What triggers a corrective action plan? D for three consecutive years, or a single E.
When must the review of the measure be completed? By 1 January 2026, under regulation 28.11.
Which SEEMP guidelines apply? The 2024 guidelines, MEPC.395(82).

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Hold the mechanism as three words in order: ATTAINED, REQUIRED, RATED — what the ship did, what it was supposed to do, and the letter that follows. The letter grades are the five words of regulation 28.6: major superior, minor superior, moderate, minor inferior, inferior.
For the guidelines, count them in the order the calculation runs: G1 how to calculate it, G2 what to compare it to, G3 how much to tighten it, G4 how to grade it, G5 what may be adjusted.
For the reduction factors, the odd numbers climb by two — 5, 7, 9, 11 for 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026. This sitting is the 9.

For the improvement measures, work down the formula: the numerator is fuel and its carbon, the denominator is capacity and distance. Everything you can do is in one of those two places — or in the quality of the numbers themselves.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28 — Operational carbon intensity. Introduced by resolution MEPC.328(76), the 2021 revised Annex VI, in force 1 November 2022.
Reg 28.1, 28.2 — calculate after the end of 2023 and each following year, 1 January to 31 December; report within three months. Reg 27 — the DCS, from calendar year 2019.
Reg 28.4 — Required CII = (1 − Z/100) × CIIR. Reg 28.6 — ratings A to E; the middle point of C is the required CII; assigned by the Administration or an organization duly authorized by it.

Reg 28.7 to 28.9 — D for three consecutive years or E: corrective action plan, SEEMP revised and submitted within one month of reporting, actions undertaken. Reg 28.10 — incentives encouraged for A and B.
Reg 28.11 — review to be completed by 1 January 2026, including revision of Z and CIIR.
Reg 26 — the SEEMP, its content and its verification.

G1 — MEPC.352(78): indicators and calculation; AER and cgDIST as supply-based CII; EEOI at section 5 for trial purposes. G2 — MEPC.353(78): reference lines. G3 — MEPC.338(76): reduction factors, table 1. G4 — MEPC.354(78): rating boundaries. G5 — MEPC.355(78): correction factors and voyage adjustments.
MEPC.395(82), 4 October 2024 — the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, superseding MEPC.346(78). MEPC.1/Circ.684 — EEOI guidelines.
MEPC.385(81) — adopted 22 March 2024, accepted 1 February 2025, in force 1 August 2025; operative paragraph 4 invites early application of the revised appendix IX DCS data from 1 January 2025.
MEPC.400(83) — adopted 11 April 2025; replaced G3 table 1, leaving 2023 to 2026 unchanged and supplying 2027 to 2030.
Context: MEPC.377(80), the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted 7 July 2023.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, currency and a corpus correction request

blocks.p: No numeric rating boundary and no reference-line coefficient is quoted. This is not caution but a rule: the corpus’s own canonical record for regulation 28 states that the Annex fixes only that the middle point of rating level C equals the required annual operational CII, prints no band width and no boundary value, and that the boundaries are not derivable from the corpus and no value may be supplied for them from any source. The answer explains the mechanism and names the guideline that carries the figures.

No percentage saving is attributed to any improvement measure. Gains from hull cleaning, propeller polishing, energy saving devices, air lubrication, wind assistance or speed reduction are installation-specific and vendor-sourced. Mechanism and direction only.

No body text of MARPOL Annex VI is reproduced. The Annex is held frozen and citation-ready in the corpus, with a facts-and-pointers export policy; identity, structure, numerics, duty-bearers and temporal facts are used, and the wording above is the answer’s own.

A TRUE_SOURCE_CORRECTION_REQUEST is raised and has not been actioned locally. Three canonical corpus records — the Annex VI amendment register and the canonical records for regulations 26 and 28 — give the entry into force of MEPC.328(76) as 1 November 2023. It is 1 November 2022, stated in that resolution’s own operative paragraph 3 and corroborated in the recitals of two further held resolutions, MEPC.352(78) and MEPC.346(78). QP production never edits True Source, so the corpus was not modified and no frozen record was touched; this answer uses 1 November 2022 and the defect is reported for the Founder’s decision.

Currency. Every instrument cited is in the state it was in at this sitting: G1, G2, G4 and G5 from MEPC 78 and G3 from MEPC 76; the 2024 SEEMP guidelines; MEPC.385(81) accepted but not in force; MEPC.400(83) adopted during this month and shown to be immaterial to the 2025 factor; the regulation 28.11 review not reported; and the Net-Zero Framework absent, having been approved but never adopted. MEPC.392(82), whose entry into force is 1 March 2026, and every instrument of the 34th Assembly of December 2025, are deliberately absent.

notes: The intake flagged IMO INSTRUMENT IN FLUX at MEDIUM. The flag is REAL and resolves to a precise April 2025 position rather than being cleared. This is the most temporally dense question on the paper.

THE SCHEME IS IN ITS THIRD YEAR AT THIS SITTING, NOT ITS FIRST. Calendar year 2023 was the first measured year under regulation 28.1; its attained CII was reportable by 31 March 2024 and ratings for 2023 have been assigned. The attained CII for calendar year 2024 fell due for reporting by 31 MARCH 2025 - in the month immediately before this sitting. A donor written for a January 2024 sitting says no ship has yet been rated, and that is FALSE here.
THE OPERATIVE REDUCTION FACTOR IS Z = 9% FOR 2025, relative to the 2019 reference line. The donor's 7% is the 2024 figure.

NO SHIP CAN YET HAVE BEEN RATED D FOR THREE CONSECUTIVE YEARS. The first possible three-year run is 2023, 2024 and 2025, and 2025 is incomplete at this sitting. So at April 2025 the ONLY live trigger for regulation 28.7 is a single E rating. That is a precise and examinable sitting-relative fact and it is stated in the answer.

SEEMP GUIDELINE SUPERSESSION: MEPC.346(78), the 2022 SEEMP Guidelines, were SUPERSEDED by MEPC.395(82), the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines adopted 4 OCTOBER 2024 - six months before this sitting. A January 2024 donor cites the 2022 guidelines as current and is wrong here. This was found by the QP2410-Q8 cross-check, not by inspection of the stems.

MEPC.385(81): adopted 22 March 2024, DEEMED ACCEPTED 1 FEBRUARY 2025, ENTERS INTO FORCE 1 AUGUST 2025. At this sitting it is ACCEPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE. Its operative paragraph 4 INVITES early application of the revised appendix IX DCS data from 1 January 2025 - an invitation, not a duty, and the distinction is stated expressly.

THE IN-MONTH BOUNDARY, AND WHY IT DOES NOT MATTER. MEPC.400(83) was adopted on 11 APRIL 2025, inside this sitting month, and replaced G3 table 1. The examination day is not printed on the source copy, so the relation between the sitting and 11 April is UNKNOWABLE. It is nevertheless immaterial, and that is PROVED rather than assumed: MEPC.400(83) left the 2023 to 2026 rows unchanged at 5, 7, 9 and 11 per cent and supplied only the previously blank 2027 to 2030 figures. Z = 9% FOR 2025 IS CORRECT ON EVERY DAY OF APRIL 2025. The answer states the 2025 factor and rests no scoring proposition on the 2027 to 2030 figures.

THE IMO NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK IS PROHIBITED. It was APPROVED at MEPC 83 on 11 April 2025 - inside this month - and was never adopted; the extraordinary session of October 2025 adjourned without adopting anything. On an early-April sitting day it was not even approved. It is not mentioned as operative, as adopted, or as pending entry into force, and because the day is unknown the answer does not assert that approval had happened either.
MEPC.392(82) is ADOPTED with entry into force 1 March 2026 and is absent. The 34th Assembly (3 December 2025) postdates this sitting and every A.1xxx(34) instrument is absent.
REGULATION 28.11 REVIEW: required to be completed by 1 January 2026 and NOT reported at this sitting. Nothing is asserted about its conclusions.

CORPUS DEFECT RAISED: three canonical corpus records give MEPC.328(76)'s entry into force as 2023-11-01. The resolution's own operative paragraph 3 says 1 NOVEMBER 2022, corroborated by two further held resolutions. This answer uses 1 November 2022 and a TRUE_SOURCE_CORRECTION_REQUEST is recorded. The corpus was not modified.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: One unlimbed 16-mark question setting THREE tasks - explain the CII rating concept, critically discuss AER and EEOI, and give the measures to improve the rating - and the middle one is where the marks are. 'Critically discuss' is not 'describe': a candidate who defines both metrics and stops has answered half of the highest-value task. The examiner is testing whether the candidate understands that CII is a comparison against a MOVING target, and that the choice of metric is contestable.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as a single block with no sub-division. Three tasks. The critical discussion of AER and EEOI is the discriminating task and carries the largest share of writing; the improvement measures are the easiest marks and must not consume the answer, since a long undifferentiated list scores no better than a short structured one. The mechanism must come first because the critical discussion is unintelligible without it.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate can write the required-CII formula, give the reduction factor FOR THIS YEAR, state where rating C sits, know exactly what a D or an E triggers and what it does not, and explain WHY the regulation uses a capacity proxy rather than actual cargo. Naming G1 to G5 and what each supplies is the mark of someone who has opened the instruments. At this sitting, knowing that ratings now exist - and that no three-year D run is yet possible - is the currency discriminator.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - and higher than on any other question on this paper. The scheme moves every single year by design, because Z tightens annually, and three of the donor's four sitting-relative statements are false at this sitting. On top of that, the sitting month itself contains the adoption of MEPC.400(83), so the question sits directly on an in-month instrument boundary. The controls are that the answer states the year's Z factor explicitly, states where the scheme has reached in its own lifecycle, and rests nothing on the 2027 to 2030 figures.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. MARPOL Annex VI applies through the flag State and India is a Party. No Indian statute is load-bearing and the Merchant Shipping Act position is not engaged.
technical_ambiguities: Whether AER measures transport work or merely distance - it measures distance, with capacity as a proxy for cargo
Whether EEOI is mandatory - it is not; G1 section 5 lists it for trial purposes
Whether a single D rating has consequences - it does not; three consecutive years, or an E, is the trigger
Whether any ship could have been rated D for three consecutive years at this sitting - it could not, because the earliest possible run is 2023 to 2025 and 2025 is incomplete
Whether CII carries a penal sanction - it does not; regulation 28 prints no withdrawal, no rejection and no sanction, and the pressure is commercial and administrative
Whether time at anchor helps or harms AER - it harms it, and this is the clearest single test of understanding

Then the improvement measures in two sections, operational before technical, closing on the two levers candidates never mention - data quality and the G5 adjustments - and on the SEEMP as the place all of it is administered. questions.understand_first: CII does something none of the older MARPOL rules do: it grades how the ship is operated, every year, and the pass mark moves. The ship's own fuel and distance figures, already reported to the flag State since 2019, are turned into a number; that number is compared with a target derived from the 2019 industry average and tightened by a percentage that grows each year; and the comparison produces a letter from A to E. Everything else follows. The reason AER and EEOI are worth arguing about is that the whole scheme rests on how you measure transport work, and IMO deliberately chose the measure it could audit — capacity times distance — over the measure that is actually true — cargo times distance. And the reason the improvement measures are not an arbitrary list is that the metric is a fraction: you can attack the numerator, the denominator, or the quality of the numbers, and nothing else. At this sitting there is one more thing to hold: the scheme is no longer theoretical. Ships carry ratings, the second measured year is closed and its data has already fallen due, and the ratchet has moved from 5 % to 9 %.

steps.title: Where CII sits in law, and where the scheme has reached
points: regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, introduced by the 2021 revised Annex VI, resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022
the OPERATIONAL half of the short-term GHG measure; EEXI at regulation 23 is the technical half
EEXI is assessed once on design; CII is assessed every year on operation
applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above in the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1
reg 28.1 - calculate the attained annual operational CII after the end of calendar year 2023 and each following year, over 1 January to 31 December
reg 28.2 - report it to the Administration within three months of the year end
reg 27 - the data comes from the IMO DCS, running since calendar year 2019
AT THIS SITTING: 2023 and 2024 are both complete measured years
ratings for 2023 have been assigned, and the attained CII for 2024 fell due for reporting by 31 MARCH 2025 - in the month immediately before this examination
the SEEMP guidance is now the 2024 edition, MEPC.395(82) of 4 October 2024, which superseded MEPC.346(78)

steps.title: The mechanism - attained, required, Z and the reference line
points: the rating is a COMPARISON, not an absolute measurement
attained annual operational CII = total mass of CO2 emitted (M) divided by total transport work undertaken (W) in the calendar year
M is the sum of CO2 from all fuel oil consumed, from DCS fuel figures multiplied by the fuel-to-CO2 conversion factor for each fuel type
reg 28.4 - Required CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference
the CII reference is the 2019 reference line value for the ship type, under G2, MEPC.353(78)
Z is the annual reduction factor and is what makes the standard tighten
AT THIS SITTING THE OPERATIVE FACTOR IS 9 % FOR 2025
the 2027 to 2030 factors were printed blank in G3 and were supplied by MEPC.400(83), adopted 11 April 2025 - the same month as this sitting - which left 2023 to 2026 unchanged
so the same operating pattern earns a worse rating every year, because the target moves and the ship does not

steps.title: The rating, and what actually attaches to it
points: reg 28.6 - ratings A to E: major superior, minor superior, moderate, minor inferior, inferior
reg 28.6 - the middle point of rating level C IS the required annual operational CII
the rating is determined by the Administration, or any organization duly authorized by it, from the attained CII verified against the required CII

G4, MEPC.354(78), places the boundaries around that midpoint, and its design intent is a fleet distribution - middle 30 % at C, upper 20 % and further 15 % at D and E, lower 20 % and further 15 % at B and A
NO BOUNDARY VALUE IS QUOTED - the Annex fixes only the midpoint of C, and the boundaries are ship-type specific guideline tables
reg 28.7 - a ship rated D for THREE CONSECUTIVE YEARS, or rated E, develops a plan of corrective actions
reg 28.8 - the SEEMP is reviewed to include it and submitted for verification no later than ONE MONTH after reporting the attained CII
reg 28.9 - the actions must be duly undertaken; reg 28.10 - incentives are ENCOURAGED for A and B, which is hortatory and creates no entitlement
AT THIS SITTING NO SHIP CAN YET HAVE THREE CONSECUTIVE D RATINGS - the earliest possible run is 2023, 2024 and 2025, and 2025 is incomplete
so the only live trigger for regulation 28.7 in April 2025 is a single E rating
regulation 28 prints NO detention, NO fine, NO certificate withdrawal and no sanction at all - the pressure is commercial and administrative
reg 28.11 - a review to be completed by 1 January 2026, which had not reported at this sitting

steps.title: AER - what it measures and why the regulation uses it
points: G1, MEPC.352(78), draws the distinction the question is really about
a DEMAND-BASED CII uses the actual mass or volume of cargo carried
a SUPPLY-BASED CII uses the ship's capacity as a PROXY for cargo
AER - the Annual Efficiency Ratio - is the supply-based CII which uses DWT as the capacity; cgDIST is the same idea using GT
numerator - total CO2 from all fuel consumed in the calendar year, from DCS data
denominator - the ship's capacity multiplied by total distance travelled
DWT is the capacity for bulk carriers, tankers, container ships, gas carriers, LNG carriers, general cargo ships, refrigerated cargo carriers and combination carriers
GT is the capacity for cruise passenger ships, ro-ro cargo ships including vehicle carriers, and ro-ro passenger ships
its virtue is entirely practical - every input is already reported, auditable and comparable
nothing new has to be measured and two sister ships can be compared on identical terms

steps.title: EEOI, and the critical comparison
points: EEOI - the Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator - is defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684
it measures CO2 per tonne of cargo ACTUALLY CARRIED per mile - the demand-based metric
it is a truer measure of transport work: a ship that sails full has done more work than one in ballast, and EEOI says so where AER does not
its status must be stated exactly - G1 section 3.2 and section 5 list it, with EEPI, cbDIST and clDIST, among indicators encouraged for TRIAL PURPOSES only
it is voluntary; regulation 28 is satisfied by the supply-based indicator
THE CASE AGAINST AER - it rewards distance, not cargo; ballast legs and idle days at anchor both worsen it
it is blind to utilisation - a full ship and a half-empty ship score the same on the same fuel and distance
it penalises short-sea and multi-port trades where port time dominates and sea distance is small
it can be gamed at the margin by slow steaming with more ships, which lowers each ship's AER while the cargo moves no more efficiently overall
THE CASE FOR IT ANYWAY - EEOI needs cargo mass the DCS does not collect, which is commercially confidential, not verifiable by an Administration, and not comparable across trades
a car carrier, a container ship and a crude tanker cannot be ranked on tonne-miles
IMO chose the ENFORCEABLE metric over the VALID one - enforceability bought at the cost of validity
and reg 28.11 puts the CII reference and Z values inside its own review, which is IMO conceding the metric is provisional

steps.title: Operational measures to improve the rating
points: because the metric is fuel over capacity-distance, only two things are possible - burn less, or travel further for it
operational measures dominate because they are available now and cost little
SPEED AND VOYAGE MANAGEMENT - consumption rises far faster than speed, so optimising speed to the required arrival time is the largest single lever
just-in-time arrival converts waiting at anchor - which burns fuel and adds no distance - into a slower, cheaper passage
HULL AND PROPELLER CONDITION - in-water cleaning and propeller polishing planned against measured performance, not a calendar
TRIM AND DRAUGHT optimisation against the ship's own trim data, and optimum ballast - carry no more than is needed
WEATHER ROUTEING to avoid added resistance, and autopilot tuning to cut rudder-induced drag
MACHINERY AND AUXILIARY LOAD - shut down surplus generators, use the shaft generator, run pumps and fans on variable frequency drives, manage cargo heating and inert gas, control HVAC and lighting
REDUCE PORT AND IDLE CONSUMPTION - shore power where available, minimise boiler use, avoid unnecessary main engine running

steps.title: Technical, fuel and calculation measures, and where they are administered
points: TECHNICAL RETROFIT - low-friction and foul-release hull coatings; propeller retrofit or upgrade; energy saving devices such as ducts, fins and rudder bulbs
engine derating with engine or shaft power limitation; waste heat recovery; air lubrication; wind assistance
each must be justified for the specific ship and trade - none is universally worthwhile, and no percentage saving is quoted
FUEL - the numerator is CO2, not fuel mass, so switching to a lower carbon factor fuel reduces attained CII directly for the same energy delivered
DATA QUALITY - the attained CII is only as good as the reported fuel and distance, so flowmeter calibration, consistent bunker figures and correct noon-report distances matter directly to the rating
and the DCS data regime is itself moving - MEPC.385(81) replaces appendix IX and INVITES early application from 1 January 2025, though it does not enter into force until 1 August 2025

G5, MEPC.355(78) - voyage adjustments deduct fuel and the associated distance for qualifying periods; correction factors adjust the numerator or denominator for cases such as ice conditions and ship-to-ship operations
G5 states its own boundary - their use should in no way undermine the goal of reducing the carbon intensity of international shipping
ALL OF IT IS ADMINISTERED THROUGH THE SEEMP - reg 26.3 - now developed against the 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, MEPC.395(82)
the SEEMP carries the calculation methodology, the required CII for the next three years, an implementation plan and a self-evaluation procedure, and is subject to verification and company audit
that is where an examiner expects the measures to live, not in a loose list

questions.memory_cue: The mechanism is three words in order — ATTAINED, REQUIRED, RATED (steps 1, 2, 3). The argument is two metrics — AER the enforceable one (4), EEOI the true one (5). The measures follow the fraction — numerator and denominator, operational first (6), then technical, fuel and data (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: CII is regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, from the 2021 revised Annex VI (MEPC.328(76)), in force 1 November 2022, applying to ships of 5,000 GT and above. Calculate the attained CII after each calendar year from DCS data (reg 27, since 2019) and report within three months. Required CII = (1 − Z/100) × CII reference, the reference being the 2019 line under G2, and Z being 5, 7, 9, 11 per cent for 2023 to 2026 under G3 — 9 % for 2025. Rating A to E; the middle point of C is the required CII; G4 sets the boundaries. D for three consecutive years, or a single E, means a corrective action plan in the SEEMP submitted within one month of reporting; incentives are encouraged for A and B; there is no detention, fine or sanction. At this sitting ratings for 2023 exist, 2024 was reported by 31 March 2025, and no three-year D run is yet possible — so only a single E bites. AER is the supply-based CII using DWT as a proxy for cargo — the regulatory metric; cgDIST uses GT. EEOI (MEPC.1/Circ.684) uses actual cargo and is voluntary, for trial purposes under G1 section 5. The critical point: IMO chose the enforceable metric over the valid one. Improve by speed and voyage management, hull and propeller condition, trim and ballast, auxiliary load, retrofit and fuel switching — plus DCS data quality and the G5 adjustments, all administered through the SEEMP under the 2024 guidelines MEPC.395(82).
keywords: Required CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference
critical_numbers: Regulation 28 applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above
Reduction factor Z relative to the 2019 reference line: 5 % in 2023, 7 % in 2024, 9 % in 2025, 11 % in 2026
MEPC.400(83), adopted 11 April 2025, supplied 2027 to 2030 and left 2023 to 2026 unchanged
Attained CII reported within three months after the end of the calendar year - so 2024 was due by 31 March 2025
Revised SEEMP submitted no later than one month after reporting the attained CII
D for three consecutive years, or E in one year, triggers corrective action
Five rating grades; G4's design intent is middle 30 % at C, upper 20 % and further 15 % at D and E
IMO DCS data collected from calendar year 2019 under regulation 27
Review of the measure to be completed by 1 January 2026 under regulation 28.11
MEPC.385(81): deemed accepted 1 February 2025, in force 1 August 2025, early DCS application invited from 1 January 2025
quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28. Regulation 28.4 gives the required annual operational CII as (1 − Z/100) × CII reference; regulation 28.6 gives the A to E rating and fixes the middle point of rating level C at the required annual operational CII, the rating being determined by the Administration or any organization duly authorized by it; and regulations 28.7 to 28.9 require a plan of corrective actions in the SEEMP, submitted for verification no later than one month after reporting, for a ship rated D for three consecutive years or rated E.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing the answer in the scheme's first-year frame. At an April 2025 sitting, ratings for calendar year 2023 already exist and the 2024 attained CII fell due for reporting by 31 March 2025, so “no ship has yet been rated” is false; the reduction factor is 9 % for 2025, not 7 %; and the SEEMP guidance is the 2024 edition MEPC.395(82), not the 2022 one. The paired traps are treating EEOI as a regulatory requirement when G1 lists it for trial purposes only, and saying a single D rating triggers corrective action — it is D for three consecutive years or a single E, and at this sitting a three-year run is not yet arithmetically possible.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regulation is CII, where did it come from, and which ships does it catch?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, introduced by the 2021 revised Annex VI, resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above falling into the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1. It is the operational half of the short-term measure; EEXI at regulation 23 is the technical half.
retrieval_cards.why: The regulation number and the tonnage threshold are the two cheapest marks in the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Write the required CII formula and give the reduction factor for this sitting's year.
retrieval_cards.answer: Required annual operational CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference, the reference being the 2019 reference line value for the ship type under G2. Under G3, MEPC.338(76) table 1, Z is 5 % for 2023, 7 % for 2024, 9 % for 2025 and 11 % for 2026. At an April 2025 sitting the operative factor is 9 %.
retrieval_cards.why: Getting the current year's Z right is what shows the answer is anchored to its own sitting rather than inherited.

retrieval_cards.prompt: At an April 2025 sitting, how far has the CII scheme actually got?
retrieval_cards.answer: Into its third year. Calendar 2023 and 2024 are both complete measured years; ratings for 2023 have been assigned; and the 2024 attained CII fell due for reporting by 31 March 2025 under the three-month rule - in the month immediately before the paper. Crucially, no ship can yet have been rated D for three consecutive years, because the earliest possible run is 2023 to 2025 and 2025 is incomplete. So the only live trigger for regulation 28.7 is a single E.
retrieval_cards.why: A great deal of published material was written in the scheme's first year and says no ship has been rated. That is wrong here.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is AER, and what does it use as its denominator?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Annual Efficiency Ratio - the supply-based CII which uses deadweight tonnage as the capacity. The numerator is total CO2 from all fuel consumed in the calendar year; the denominator is the ship's capacity multiplied by the total distance travelled. The variant using gross tonnage instead of DWT is cgDIST, used for cruise passenger, ro-ro cargo and ro-ro passenger ships.
retrieval_cards.why: Supply-based means capacity is a PROXY for cargo, and every strength and weakness of AER follows from that one substitution.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish AER from EEOI and state the status of each.
retrieval_cards.answer: AER is supply-based: it uses the ship's capacity as a proxy for cargo, takes every input from the IMO DCS, and is the metric by which regulation 28 is satisfied. EEOI is demand-based: it uses the cargo actually carried, is defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684, and under G1 section 5 is encouraged for trial purposes only. EEOI is voluntary.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the whole of the critical limb, and treating EEOI as mandatory is the commonest error in it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did IMO regulate with AER when EEOI is the better measure of transport work?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because EEOI requires cargo mass data which the DCS does not collect, which is commercially confidential, which an Administration cannot verify as it verifies fuel and distance, and which is not comparable across ship types. AER's inputs are already reported, already audited and already comparable. IMO chose the enforceable metric over the valid one - and regulation 28.11 puts the reference values and Z factors inside its own review, which concedes the choice is provisional.
retrieval_cards.why: 'Critically discuss' is asking for this trade-off, not for a list of AER's flaws.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a ship rated D, and what happens to one rated E?
retrieval_cards.answer: A single D does nothing, and two do nothing. It is D for three consecutive years, or E in any one year, that triggers regulation 28.7: the ship develops a plan of corrective actions, the SEEMP is reviewed to include it and submitted to the Administration no later than one month after reporting the attained CII, and the actions must be duly undertaken. There is no detention, fine or certificate withdrawal - regulation 28 prints no sanction at all.
retrieval_cards.why: The three-consecutive-years condition and the total absence of a penal sanction are both routinely got wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does rating C sit relative to the required CII, and can you state the band boundaries?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 28.6 - the middle point of rating level C is the value equivalent to the required annual operational CII. C is the target itself, not a pass mark below it. The boundaries cannot be stated from the Annex: it fixes only that midpoint and prints no band width or boundary value. The boundaries are ship-type-specific tables in G4, MEPC.354(78), whose design intent is that the middle 30 % of a segment falls in C.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the whole fleet cannot simply settle at C as the standard tightens - and why quoting a boundary number is a mistake.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five CII guidelines and what each supplies.
retrieval_cards.answer: G1, MEPC.352(78) - the indicators and the calculation method. G2, MEPC.353(78) - the reference lines. G3, MEPC.338(76) - the reduction factors. G4, MEPC.354(78) - the rating boundaries. G5, MEPC.355(78) - correction factors and voyage adjustments. They run in the order the calculation runs: calculate, compare, tighten, grade, adjust.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming them and what each does is the clearest sign a candidate has opened the instruments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A ship spends three weeks at anchor awaiting a berth. What does that do to its AER?
retrieval_cards.answer: It worsens it. Fuel is burned, so the numerator grows, while no distance is travelled, so the denominator does not. Time at anchor is pure penalty under AER - which is exactly why just-in-time arrival, converting waiting into a slower passage, is one of the strongest operational measures.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the sharpest single illustration that AER measures distance covered, not work done.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give three ways to improve CII that do not involve modifying the ship.
retrieval_cards.answer: Speed and voyage management, especially just-in-time arrival; improving the quality of the DCS fuel and distance data on which the attained CII is calculated; and applying the G5 voyage adjustments and correction factors where the ship genuinely qualifies, for example ice conditions or ship-to-ship operations. G5 adds that their use must in no way undermine the goal of reducing carbon intensity.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows the metric is a fraction with three attackable parts, not just a fuel bill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SEEMP guidelines apply at this sitting, and what must the SEEMP contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2024 Guidelines for the development of a SEEMP, resolution MEPC.395(82), adopted 4 October 2024, which superseded the 2022 guidelines MEPC.346(78). Under regulation 26 an affected ship's SEEMP must carry the methodology for calculating the attained CII and the reporting process, the required CII for the next three years, an implementation plan for achieving it, and a procedure for self-evaluation and improvement - and it is subject to verification and company audit.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the 2022 guidelines is exactly the error a stem-identical January 2024 donor would carry forward.

retrieval_cards.prompt: An instrument was adopted during this examination month. Does it change the answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: MEPC.400(83) was adopted on 11 April 2025 and replaced the G3 reduction-factor table. It does not change the answer: it left 2023 to 2026 unchanged at 5, 7, 9 and 11 per cent and supplied only the previously blank 2027 to 2030 figures. Z remains 9 % for 2025 whichever day in April the paper was sat. Separately, the IMO Net-Zero Framework was approved at the same session but never adopted, and has no place in a regulation 28 answer.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the paper's in-month boundary, and the discipline is to check whether the change reaches the question rather than to guess the date.
