questions.understand_first: A P&I club is not an insurance company and the whole answer turns on that. It is a mutual: a group of shipowners who have agreed to carry each other’s third-party liabilities, who own the club themselves, and who therefore pay calls rather than premiums — because a call is what a member of an association contributes, not what a customer pays a supplier. There is no external shareholder taking a profit, so a good year is retained for the members and a bad year is paid for by them. The second organising idea is the boundary of the cover: the club insures liability to other people, and it does not insure the member’s own loss. Hull and machinery damage belongs to the hull underwriter; lost earnings belong to a loss-of-hire policy; the club answers for the crewman injured, the cargo damaged, the pier struck, the oil spilled and the wreck to be removed. And the third idea, which the third limb is about, is why the club is present at the incident at all: because a maritime claim can arrest the ship, and the club’s letter of undertaking is what substitutes for the ship as security so the ship can sail.

steps.title: What a P&I club is - the mutual
points: a Protection and Indemnity club is a MUTUAL ASSOCIATION of shipowners, charterers and operators formed to cover THIRD-PARTY LIABILITIES arising from the operation of their ships
the members ARE the club - there are no external shareholders and no profit is taken out
so it is not a company selling a product to a customer; it is a group of owners sharing each other's liabilities
the consequence: an underwriting surplus is retained for the members, and a deficit is met by them
hence CALLS, not premiums - a call is what a member of an association contributes
the cover is LIABILITY cover, and it is not a fixed sum insured - it is the liability the member incurs, subject to the rules
that distinguishes it from ordinary fixed-premium marine insurance in three ways - mutuality, breadth of cover, and the absence of a fixed sum insured
the club is governed by its members through a board of directors drawn from the membership, and managed day to day by professional managers
twelve clubs participate in the International Group, which is the industry body through which the largest claims are shared

steps.title: How the club collects funds
points: funding is in TIERS, and the tiers are the answer to 'how do they collect fund from ship-owners'
ADVANCE CALL - levied on entry for the policy year, and paid in instalments
it is assessed on the member's ENTERED TONNAGE and rated for ship type, trade and area of operation, crew nationality and terms, and above all the member's CLAIMS RECORD
SUPPLEMENTARY CALL - levied if the policy year's claims and expenses exceed the advance calls plus investment income
this is the mutual mechanism working as designed, not a penalty - the members carry the year between them
RELEASE CALL - payable by a member leaving the club, buying out its exposure to future supplementary calls on the open policy years
policy years are kept open for several years because liability claims take years to mature, which is why the release call exists at all
DEDUCTIBLES - the member bears an agreed first amount of each claim, which controls small-claim frequency
ABOVE THE CLUB: the INTERNATIONAL GROUP POOLING AGREEMENT shares claims exceeding each club's own retention across the participating clubs
above the pool sits the GROUP'S COLLECTIVE REINSURANCE, and above that a further overspill layer
so a single very large claim is met by the whole group rather than by one club - which is what makes cover of that size possible at all
note the statute's own recognition of the mechanism - the Admiralty Act 2017 lists at section 4(1)(s) 'insurance premium (including mutual insurance calls)' as a maritime claim

steps.title: The risks covered under 'protection'
points: PROTECTION covers liabilities connected with the OPERATION OF THE SHIP other than cargo - broadly, people and the ship's interaction with the world
CREW - personal injury, illness and death; medical and hospital expenses; repatriation; loss of personal effects; and crew wages in defined circumstances
OTHER PERSONS - injury to and death of stevedores, pilots, visitors, passengers and third parties
COLLISION - the proportion of collision liability NOT covered by the hull and machinery policy, which classically covers only three-fourths
FIXED AND FLOATING OBJECTS - damage to piers, jetties, berths, buoys, cables and navigational aids
POLLUTION - liability for oil and other pollution, and the cost of clean-up and preventive measures, beyond what the hull cover reaches
WRECK REMOVAL - the cost of raising, removing, destroying or marking the wreck where that is legally compelled
STOWAWAYS, REFUGEES AND PERSONS RESCUED AT SEA - maintenance and repatriation costs
QUARANTINE and disinfection expenses arising from infectious disease on board
FINES - for pollution, for cargo shortage or overlanding, for immigration and customs breaches, and for breaches of safety or navigation rules, so far as the rules permit
TOWAGE and salvage liabilities under approved contracts, and the member's liability under approved indemnities
LEGAL COSTS of investigating, defending or settling any of the above

steps.title: The risks covered under 'indemnity' - and the boundary of the cover
points: INDEMNITY covers the member's liability to CARGO
loss of, damage to, shortage of and contamination of cargo carried, arising from breach of the contract of carriage
cargo's proportion of GENERAL AVERAGE where it cannot be recovered from cargo interests because of a breach of the contract
liabilities arising under approved bill of lading and charterparty terms, and under through and combined transport documents
the historical division is simple: PROTECTION is people and the outside world, INDEMNITY is the goods you carried
NOW STATE THE BOUNDARY, because the marks are as much in what is excluded as in what is covered
the club covers LIABILITY, not the member's own loss - so hull and machinery damage, and loss of hire, are NOT club risks
cargo the member owns is not a club risk, because there is no liability to a third party
cover is conditioned on the ship being CLASSED with an approved society and MAINTAINED IN CLASS, and on flag and statutory certification being maintained
and on the member conducting the claim as the rules require - prompt notice, no admission of liability, evidence preserved
PAY TO BE PAID - in principle the club indemnifies a liability the member has DISCHARGED, so the member pays first and is reimbursed
that is relaxed in practice, and displaced by statute where a compulsory-insurance regime gives the claimant a DIRECT ACTION against the insurer
the club issues the BLUE CARD evidencing that compulsory insurance - for CLC 1992, the Bunkers Convention, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention and the MLC financial security standards

steps.title: How the club handles a claim
points: the club is not a passive payer of invoices - it takes CONDUCT of the claim
THE CORRESPONDENT is the first mechanism - a local representative the club appoints in ports worldwide
on notification the correspondent attends the ship, protects the member's position, and appoints surveyors, lawyers and experts locally
that is why a club is worth more than its balance sheet: it puts a competent, instructed person on the quay within hours, anywhere
THE CLAIMS EXECUTIVE in the club takes conduct of substantial claims - assessing liability and quantum, instructing lawyers, negotiating and settling
the club investigates whether liability exists at all before it pays anything, and defends where it does not
SECURITY is the club's most valuable single service - a maritime claim can arrest the ship under section 5 of the Admiralty Act 2017
the club issues a LETTER OF UNDERTAKING to the claimant, substituting the club's covenant for the ship as security
that lifts or prevents the arrest and lets the ship sail - and it is not a payment or an admission
the club also advises the member throughout - on the SMS response, on dealing with authorities, and on preserving privilege
and it applies the deductible, the pooling arrangement and the reinsurance layers behind the scenes, which the member never sees
SUBROGATION - having indemnified, the club steps into the member's rights of recovery against third parties, a general marine insurance principle

steps.title: The procedure for filing a claim
points: state it as a SEQUENCE, because the question asks for a procedure
1. IMMEDIATE NOTIFICATION - notify the club, through the managers or the local correspondent, without delay. Prompt notice is a CONDITION of the cover
2. DO NOT ADMIT LIABILITY - and do not sign any document accepting responsibility or quantum. Sign for receipt only
3. THE CORRESPONDENT ATTENDS - and appoints a surveyor to establish the facts while they still exist
4. PRESERVE AND GATHER EVIDENCE - this is where the claim is won or lost, and it is largely the ship's work
5. SUBMIT THE FORMAL CLAIM to the club with the supporting documentation, quantified, with the member's account of the incident
6. THE CLUB ASSESSES cover, liability and quantum - is this a covered risk under the rules, is the member liable, and for how much
7. SECURITY IS PUT UP where an arrest is threatened - the letter of undertaking
8. NEGOTIATION, SETTLEMENT OR DEFENCE - the club conducts it, and may litigate or arbitrate where liability is denied
9. PAYMENT AND REIMBURSEMENT - the deductible is borne by the member; pooling and reinsurance operate above the club's retention
10. RECOVERY - subrogated recovery against third parties, and the claim's effect on the member's record and future calls
note that the last point closes the loop back to limb (a): the claims record rates the advance call

steps.title: What the ship - and the Chief Engineer - contributes
points: the club can only defend a claim on the evidence the ship preserved in the first hours
REPORT IMMEDIATELY through the master and the Company to the club and the correspondent
PRESERVE THE SCENE and the physical evidence - do not repair, discard or clean up the failed component before it has been surveyed
SECURE THE RECORDS - engine room logbook, bell book, alarm and event printouts, planned maintenance records, running hours, oil analysis, bunker delivery notes and sounding records
PHOTOGRAPH everything, dated, before anything is disturbed
PREPARE A FACTUAL STATEMENT - what happened, in sequence, with times. Facts and not opinion, and no speculation about cause
ATTEND THE SURVEY and make the machinery and the records available to the club's surveyor
for a MACHINERY-RELATED claim - a fuel contamination, a crankcase explosion, a blackout leading to a grounding - the engine room evidence IS the case
raise it in the SMS as a non-conformity under ISM element 9 with root cause and corrective action, because the club will be asked what was done about it
and never give a statement to a third party's surveyor or lawyer without the club's instruction

questions.memory_cue: Three words carry the question. MUTUAL — members own it, so calls not premiums (1, 2). LIABILITY — other people's losses, never your own ship (3, 4). SECURITY — the letter of undertaking that stops the arrest, which is why the club is on the quay at all (5, 6, 7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: A P&I club is a MUTUAL association of shipowners covering THIRD-PARTY LIABILITIES — the members own it, there are no shareholders, so they pay CALLS not premiums and there is no fixed sum insured. Funding in tiers: advance call on entered tonnage rated for ship type, trade, crew and claims record; supplementary call if the year's claims exceed advance calls plus investment income; release call to leave; plus deductibles. Above the club: the International Group pooling agreement (twelve clubs), then collective reinsurance, then overspill. PROTECTION = people and the outside world — crew injury, illness, death and repatriation; third-party injury; the uninsured share of collision liability; damage to fixed and floating objects; pollution and clean-up; wreck removal; stowaways; quarantine; fines; legal costs. INDEMNITY = cargo — loss, damage, shortage, contamination, and cargo's unrecoverable share of general average. NOT covered: hull and machinery damage, loss of hire, your own cargo. Conditions: in class with an approved society, certification maintained, claim conducted per the rules. Pay to be paid — displaced by direct action under CLC, Bunkers, Wreck Removal and MLC, for which the club issues the blue card. Claims: the correspondent attends and appoints surveyors and lawyers; the club assesses cover, liability and quantum, gives a letter of undertaking to lift an arrest under Admiralty Act s.5, then settles or defends, and is subrogated. Procedure: notify at once → admit nothing → preserve evidence → submit with documents → club assesses → security → settle or defend → recover.
critical_numbers: Twelve clubs participate in the International Group pooling agreement (a figure that changes with mergers)
Three kinds of call: advance, supplementary and release
Hull policies classically cover three-fourths of collision liability, the club covering the remainder
Three layers above the member: club retention, the pool, then collective reinsurance and overspill
Admiralty Act 2017 section 4(1)(s) recognises 'insurance premium (including mutual insurance calls)' as a maritime claim
No monetary limit, pool retention or reinsurance attachment point is quoted - all are reset annually
quick_revision.critical_regulation: No convention or code governs P&I clubs; they are private mutual associations. The statutory frame that matters is the Admiralty (Jurisdiction and Settlement of Maritime Claims) Act, 2017: section 4(1) lists as maritime claims the very heads a club insures against — death and personal injury, loss or damage to goods, crew wages and repatriation, environmental damage and preventive measures, wreck removal — and at section 4(1)(s) expressly recognises “insurance premium (including mutual insurance calls)”. Section 5 supplies the arrest power that makes the club's letter of undertaking commercially necessary. Alongside it, the compulsory-insurance conventions — CLC 1992, Bunkers 2001, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention and the MLC, 2006 financial security standards — give claimants a direct action and require the certificate the club's blue card supports.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating the club as an ordinary insurer and its cover as covering the ship. A club is a mutual owned by its members, funded by calls rather than premiums, and it insures liability to third parties — so hull and machinery damage, loss of hire and cargo the member owns are not club risks. A crankshaft failure is a hull claim; the grounding and oil spill it causes are P&I claims. The paired limb-(b) trap is putting cargo under “protection”: cargo liability is indemnity. And structurally, note that this sitting prints 5 + 5 + 6 where an earlier sitting printed 8 + 8 for the same first two limbs — delivering them at the old length starves the six-mark claims limb, which is the largest on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a P&I club, and how does it differ from an ordinary marine insurer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A mutual association of shipowners, charterers and operators covering the third-party liabilities arising from ship operation. The members own the club - there are no external shareholders - so a surplus is retained for them and a deficit met by them. It differs from fixed-premium insurance in three ways: mutuality, breadth of cover, and no fixed sum insured. Members pay calls, not premiums.
retrieval_cards.why: The word 'mutual' is the framing mark and everything else in limb (a) follows from it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three kinds of call and say what each is for.
retrieval_cards.answer: Advance call - levied on entry for the policy year, assessed on entered tonnage and rated for ship type, trade, crew and the member's claims record. Supplementary call - levied if the year's claims and expenses exceed the advance calls plus investment income; it is the mutual mechanism working as designed, not a penalty. Release call - payable by a member leaving, buying out its exposure to future supplementary calls on the open policy years.
retrieval_cards.why: Three calls answer 'how do they collect fund from ship-owners' completely, and the release call shows why policy years stay open.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a very large claim actually paid?
retrieval_cards.answer: In layers. The member bears the deductible; the club bears its own retention; claims above that retention are shared across the participating clubs under the International Group pooling agreement; above the pool sits the Group's collective reinsurance, and above that a further overspill layer. So a single very large claim is met by the whole group rather than by one club.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what makes cover of that magnitude possible at all, and it is routinely omitted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Split the risks between 'protection' and 'indemnity'.
retrieval_cards.answer: Protection is people and the ship's interaction with the outside world: crew injury, illness, death and repatriation; injury to third parties; the proportion of collision liability the hull policy does not cover; damage to fixed and floating objects; pollution and clean-up; wreck removal; stowaways and persons rescued; quarantine; fines; and legal costs. Indemnity is cargo: loss, damage, shortage and contamination, and cargo's proportion of general average unrecoverable from cargo interests. P for People, I for Items carried.
retrieval_cards.why: The split IS limb (b); an undifferentiated list of covered risks answers neither half.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your main engine crankshaft fails. Is that a P&I claim? What if it causes a grounding and a spill?
retrieval_cards.answer: The crankshaft damage is NOT a P&I claim - it is the member's own loss and belongs to hull and machinery cover. The club insures liability to third parties. But if the failure causes a grounding, then the pollution liability, the clean-up and preventive measures, any wreck removal and any third-party damage ARE club risks. The engine damage still is not.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the sharpest test of the liability boundary and a standard oral question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: On what conditions does club cover depend?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the ship is classed with an approved classification society and maintained in class; that flag and statutory certification are maintained; and that the member conducts the claim as the rules require - prompt notice, no admission of liability, evidence preserved. A ship out of class has a cover problem as well as a class problem.
retrieval_cards.why: Cover is conditional, and candidates who list only the covered risks miss the conditions the club actually relies on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is 'pay to be paid', and when does it not apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: The principle that the club indemnifies a liability the member has already discharged - the member pays first and is reimbursed. It is relaxed in practice and displaced by statute wherever a compulsory-insurance convention gives the claimant a direct action against the insurer: CLC 1992, the Bunkers Convention 2001, the Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention and the MLC, 2006 financial security standards. For those the club issues a blue card supporting the ship's certificate.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why a claimant can sometimes sue the club directly, and why a club that refuses a blue card can stop a ship trading.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a letter of undertaking, and is it a payment?
retrieval_cards.answer: Security given by the club to a claimant - a written promise to meet any judgment or agreed settlement up to a stated amount - which substitutes the club's covenant for the ship itself and so lifts or prevents an arrest under section 5 of the Admiralty Act 2017. It is NEITHER a payment NOR an admission of liability, which is exactly why it can be given while liability is still denied.
retrieval_cards.why: The single best discriminator in limb (c), and it links the question to the Admiralty Act question on the same paper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the procedure for filing a P&I claim.
retrieval_cards.answer: Notify the club through its managers or local correspondent without delay - prompt notice is a condition of cover. Admit no liability and sign nothing but a receipt. The correspondent attends and appoints a surveyor. Preserve and gather the evidence. Submit the formal claim with supporting documentation, quantified. The club assesses cover, liability and quantum. Security is given by letter of undertaking where arrest is threatened. The club negotiates, settles or defends. Payment follows, the member bearing the deductible. Finally, subrogated recovery against third parties - and the claim affects the member's record and future calls.
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks for a procedure, so the answer must be a sequence rather than a description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: After a machinery casualty, what must the Chief Engineer do to protect the claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: Report immediately through the master and Company to the club and correspondent. Preserve the scene - do NOT repair, discard or clean up the failed component before it is surveyed. Secure the records: engine room logbook and bell book, alarm and event printouts, planned maintenance records, running hours, lube oil analysis, bunker delivery notes and retained samples, sounding records. Photograph everything, dated. Prepare a factual statement - times and sequence, facts not opinion, no speculation on cause. Attend the survey. Raise an ISM element 9 non-conformity. Give no statement to a third party's surveyor or lawyer without the club's instruction.
retrieval_cards.why: Engine room evidence is perishable and it IS the case in a machinery-related claim - tidying up is the single most damaging thing an engineer can do.

retrieval_cards.prompt: This sitting prints 5 + 5 + 6. Why does that matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the same first two limbs were set at 8 + 8 at an earlier sitting, so material carried over will overrun them by roughly a third. The third limb - claims handling and the procedure for filing a claim - is worth 6 marks, more than either of the others, and has no counterpart at the earlier sitting. Deliver (a) and (b) tightly and give (c) the most room.
retrieval_cards.why: The mark split is the structural fact of the question and mismanaging it costs more marks than any single point of content.

sources: PRIMARY: Resolution MSC.428(98), Maritime Cyber Risk Management in Safety Management Systems, adopted 16 June 2017, held in the True Source corpus as the sole holding of the Cyber-Risk instrument folder (sourceId TS-CYBER, constructionStatus 'held'). It affirms that an approved safety management system should take into account cyber risk management in accordance with the objectives and functional requirements of the ISM Code, and encourages Administrations to ensure that cyber risks are appropriately addressed in safety management systems NO LATER THAN THE FIRST ANNUAL VERIFICATION OF THE COMPANY'S DOCUMENT OF COMPLIANCE AFTER 1 JANUARY 2021

PRIMARY (structure): the ISM Code, made mandatory by SOLAS chapter IX - element 1.2.2 (assess all identified risks and establish appropriate safeguards), element 7 (procedures for shipboard operations), element 9 (reports and analysis of non-conformities), element 10 (maintenance of ship and equipment) and element 12 (company verification, review and evaluation) are the provisions through which cyber risk is actually managed and audited

PRIMARY (enforcement route): resolution A.1185(33), Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, held in the corpus - the machinery by which an ISM deficiency, including one arising from unaddressed cyber risk, is raised at the ship's side

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY / INTERNAL REUSE: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management, originally approved jointly by the Facilitation Committee and the Maritime Safety Committee in 2017, superseding the interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1526. The Guidelines are expressly RECOMMENDATORY. Maritime cyber risk is defined as a measure of the extent to which a technology asset could be threatened by a potential circumstance or event, which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being CORRUPTED, LOST OR COMPROMISED

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED (Rev.2 layer, from QP2403-Q5, March 2024): Rev.2 of 7 June 2022 lists EIGHT categories of vulnerable on-board system at annex 2.1.1 - bridge systems; cargo handling and management systems; propulsion, machinery management and power control systems; access control systems; passenger servicing and management systems; passenger-facing public networks; administrative and crew welfare systems; and communication systems. It sets FIVE functional elements at annex 3.5 - Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - stated to be NOT SEQUENTIAL but concurrent and continuous. It describes IT as focusing on the use of data as information and OT as focusing on the use of data to control or monitor physical processes

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED (Rev.3 layer, from QP2510-Q5, October 2025 - a POST-SITTING paper, used only because the boundary it establishes opens INSIDE this sitting month): MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 is dated 4 APRIL 2025, approved by the Maritime Safety Committee at its 108th session (May 2024) and the Facilitation Committee at its forty-ninth session (March 2025). It grows the vulnerable-systems list to NINE categories at annex 2.2.1 in a restructure; adds a SIXTH functional element, GOVERN, placed FIRST; introduces the term Computer Based System (CBS) as the organising vocabulary, covering both IT and OT systems on board; promotes IT and OT to FORMAL DEFINITIONS at annex 2.1 with worked examples; and states network segregation of OT from IT as a duty at annex 2.2.2

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY: annex 3.1 to 3.4 of the Guidelines - cyber risk management means identifying, analysing, assessing and communicating a cyber-related risk and accepting, avoiding, transferring or mitigating it to an acceptable level; the goal is OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE rather than immunity; effective cyber risk management should start at senior management level; and the approach compares the current with the desired cyber-risk posture and produces a prioritised plan

blocks.h: 1. The instrument, its status, and the edition question

blocks.p: The question names MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, the Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management. The circular was approved jointly by the Facilitation Committee and the Maritime Safety Committee in 2017, superseding the interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1526.

The Guidelines define maritime cyber risk as a measure of the extent to which a technology asset could be threatened by a potential circumstance or event, which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised. Note those three verbs: the subject is not only attack. Accident, error and failure are in scope, and availability counts as much as confidentiality.
The Guidelines are expressly recommendatory. Section 7 below explains why that does not make them optional.

On this paper the edition matters more than on any other question. Rev.2 is dated 7 June 2022. Rev.3 is dated 4 April 2025 — inside this examination month — and it changes three of the four printed limbs: the vulnerable-systems list, the number of functional elements, and the treatment of IT and OT. The source copy prints no examination day, so which edition governed the candidate in the room cannot be known.

The professional response is not to guess but to name the revision you are answering on. That is correct technique in any event — this circular has been revised repeatedly and a great deal of published material still reflects the older text — and on this paper it makes the answer defensible on either side of 4 April. Both editions are therefore identified below and each proposition is attributed. Rev.3 also introduces the organising term Computer Based System (CBS), covering both IT and OT systems on board.

blocks.h: 2. The on-board systems exposed to cyber risk

blocks.p: The Guidelines state that vulnerable systems “could include, but are not limited to” the categories listed — so this is a floor, not a closed list. The stem quotes the Guidelines’ own reasoning: it is the vulnerabilities created by accessing, interconnecting or networking these systems that create the risk.

ul: Bridge systems — navigation, safety and communication equipment: ECDIS, radar and ARPA, GNSS receivers, AIS, VDR, the integrated navigation system and the autopilot.
Cargo handling and management systems — loading computer, ballast control, cargo control room, remote level and valve control, reefer container monitoring.

Propulsion, machinery management and power control systems — engine control room and bridge control, alarm and monitoring, power management, governors, planned maintenance servers and remote vendor diagnostic links.
Access control systems — CCTV, bridge navigational watch alarm system, ship security alert system and shipboard security arrangements.
Passenger servicing and management systems — boarding, property management and passenger data systems.
Passenger-facing public networks — guest wifi and entertainment systems, which are exposed by design.
Administrative and crew welfare systems — ship administration, planned maintenance, purchasing, and crew internet and personal devices.
Communication systems — satellite communications, VoIP, email and the shore link generally.

blocks.p: Those are the eight categories as Rev.2 sets them out at annex 2.1.1. Rev.3 restructures the same ground into nine at annex 2.2.1, rewriting the headings rather than simply appending a category. Name the categories with a shipboard example each — the marks here are in the naming — and say which edition you are counting.

blocks.h: 3. What cyber risk management means, and where it starts

blocks.p: This material is unchanged between the editions, so it is the secure ground of this limb.

Cyber risk management is the process of identifying, analysing, assessing and communicating a cyber-related risk, and then accepting, avoiding, transferring or mitigating it to an acceptable level. That is the ordinary risk-management vocabulary the industry already uses — which is the whole design idea behind the Guidelines.
Three further propositions carry marks:

ol: The goal is operational resilience, not immunity. The Guidelines do not claim a ship can be made un-attackable; they aim at a ship that keeps operating, and recovers, when something goes wrong.
Effective cyber risk management should start at senior management level — not with the electro-technical officer and not with the IT department. It is a management responsibility that flows down.
Compare the current cyber-risk posture with the desired posture, and produce a prioritised plan to close the gap.

blocks.p: The controls are of three kinds — management, procedural and technical — and an answer that offers only firewalls and antivirus is an incomplete one.

blocks.h: 4. The functional elements - and how many there are

blocks.p: The Guidelines set out the functional elements and state expressly that they are not sequential: all should be concurrent and continuous and incorporated appropriately in a risk-management framework.
Under Rev.2 (7 June 2022) there are five. Under Rev.3 (4 April 2025) there are six, Govern having been added and placed first.

rows: Designate a person or entity accountable for planning, resourcing and executing cybersecurity activities, with the authority, support and expertise to do it
The systems, assets, data and capabilities which, if disrupted, pose risks to ship operations — know what you have before you defend it
Risk control processes and measures, and contingency planning, to protect against a cyber event and ensure continuity
Activities to identify a cyber event in a timely manner
Activities and plans to provide resilience and restore systems necessary for shipping operations impaired by a cyber event
Measures to back up and restore cyber systems necessary for shipping operations impacted by a cyber event

blocks.p: Together the elements constitute an ongoing process with effective feedback mechanisms, and awareness must be appropriate to each person’s role. Whichever count applies, the point that must be made is the same: do not write them as a one-pass sequence to be worked through once. That is the commonest error on this limb, and it is wrong under both editions.

blocks.h: 5. Why cyber security matters in the maritime sector

blocks.p: Argue this from the Guidelines’ own reasoning rather than from general cyber-security commentary:

ul: The risk has moved out of the physical domain. A ship can now be harmed by someone who is nowhere near it — a change in the nature of maritime risk, not merely an addition to it.
A bridge or propulsion compromise is a safety event, not an IT inconvenience. Loss of steering, propulsion, power or position is a collision, grounding or pollution risk.

IT-to-OT propagation is the classic route. A chart update carried aboard on a memory stick, or a remote diagnostic session opened to an engine vendor, crosses from the office side to the plant side. An air-gapped ship is infected by removable media.

Benign actions count. The definition covers information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised — so a mistaken software update or a failed configuration change is in scope as much as a deliberate attack.

The ship is structurally hard to defend. Mixed vendor equipment of widely different ages; a small crew with no specialist; a thin and intermittent shore link; asset lives measured in decades; and control systems that cannot simply be patched, because a machinery control system cannot be rebooted mid-passage.

Technical standards alone cannot keep up. The threat changes faster than any standard can be amended — which is precisely why the response is risk management rather than a prescriptive technical rule.
The supply chain is part of the attack surface — third-party vendors, embedded systems and maintenance laptops brought aboard.
The consequences are commercial as well as operational — charterer and vetting expectations, insurance, port and terminal requirements, and the ISM consequence set out in section 7.

blocks.h: 6. Information technology and operational technology

blocks.p: The Guidelines distinguish them by what the data is for, not by the hardware. IT focuses on the use of data as information; OT focuses on the use of data to control or monitor physical processes. Rev.3 promotes both to formal definitions at annex 2.1 and supplies worked examples, which is exactly what this limb asks for.

rows: Data to control or monitor a physical process
Ship administration and business systems; planned maintenance and purchasing; email; crew welfare and internet; personnel records; electronic manuals and certificates
Engine and machinery control and alarm systems; power management; ballast and cargo control; ECDIS and the integrated navigation system; steering gear control; refrigeration and inert gas control
Safety and availability first — the plant must keep running
Difficult — you cannot take main engine control offline for a patch cycle

blocks.p: Classify by function, not by box. A loading computer is IT when it produces a stability report and OT when it drives valve and pump control. An alarm and monitoring system is OT even though it controls nothing, because it monitors a physical process.

The examinable point is convergence. The two are no longer separate domains, and under the Rev.3 vocabulary both are Computer Based Systems. A chart update on a memory stick, a remote vendor diagnostic session, or a loading computer reading from the business network all cross the boundary. Network segregation is therefore the primary control — and Rev.3 states it as a duty at annex 2.2.2: OT systems should be segmented from IT systems, protected from Internet-facing systems, and provided with appropriate protection tools.

blocks.h: 7. How a recommendatory circular becomes a real obligation

blocks.p: This is the highest-value content in the answer and it belongs to none of the four printed limbs. Three layers, and keeping them apart is worth a mark:

ol: The obligation is resolution MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017: an approved safety management system should take account of cyber risk management in accordance with the objectives and functional requirements of the ISM Code, and Administrations were encouraged to ensure cyber risks are appropriately addressed in safety management systems no later than the first annual verification of the company’s Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021. That date is long past at this examination.
The guidance on how to do it is MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, which is recommendatory.

The detail is industry and class material — the industry Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships, IACS recommendations, ISO/IEC 27001 and the NIST Framework — named precisely because the Organization does not intend to write it, and to be used in its most current version.

blocks.p: So the position is: the guidance on how to manage cyber risk is recommendatory, but whether it is managed at all is an ISM Code matter. It is verified at Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate audit, can be written up as a non-conformity, and can become a port State control deficiency, since ISM compliance is inspectable under the Procedures for Port State Control.

A second layer applies at this sitting, and mentioning it shows real currency. IACS unified requirements UR E26 (cyber resilience of ships) and UR E27 (cyber resilience of on-board systems and equipment) apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024 — nine months before this examination. For newer tonnage, cyber resilience is a class requirement as well as an SMS one.

On board, the work lives in the ordinary ISM machinery: procedures under element 7, maintenance and software management under element 10, non-conformities, incidents and near-misses under element 9, and company review and verification under element 12. That is the honest answer to “is it mandatory?” — the circular is not; the duty is.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Sixteen marks, four printed limbs, and the paper prints the total (16) but no limb split — so budget roughly four marks each and do not let limb (A) run away with the page. (A) is a list and the marks are in the naming, with a few words of shipboard example each. (B) is the heart of the question and is really two things — the definition and posture, and the functional elements — which is why the answer splits them; that split also puts the edition-independent material first. (C) is the only discursive limb and should be anchored in the Guidelines’ own reasoning rather than in general cyber-security talk. (D) is a definitional distinction and a table earns its marks faster than prose.

Section 7 belongs to none of the four printed limbs, and it is where the best marks are. The examiner who set this question knows that the circular is recommendatory; the candidate who explains how a recommendatory circular still binds has understood the architecture rather than memorised a list.

blocks.h: The edition boundary - and how to be right without knowing the date

blocks.p: This is the hardest single thing on this paper. MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 is dated 4 April 2025 — inside this examination month. The source copy prints no examination day, so nobody can know which edition governed the candidate in the room.
And unlike the paper’s other in-month boundary, this one changes the substance of three limbs:

rows: Nine categories, annex 2.2.1 — a restructure, not an append

blocks.p: The answer to an unknowable date is not a guess and not a silent hedge. It is to name the revision you are answering on. That is correct examination technique whatever the paper — this circular has been revised repeatedly and a great deal of textbook and training material still reflects Rev.2 — and here it makes the answer defensible on both sides of 4 April. Write “answering on Rev.3 of 4 April 2025, which sets six functional elements; Rev.2, in force until that date, set five” and no examiner can mark it wrong.
The mnemonic to carry is G-IPDRR, with G for Govern understood as the April 2025 addition. Learn IPDRR alone and you are giving the previous edition’s answer without saying so.

blocks.h: The one structural idea behind the whole subject

blocks.p: Nobody wrote a Cyber Code. That is the examinable insight.

Cyber risk was brought into shipping as an extension of risk management the industry already does, not as a new technical discipline. So the response has two parts and they are deliberately different in kind: a recommendatory circular saying how, and a resolution putting the obligation inside the ISM Code saying that it must be done at all. The message was, in effect, you already have a safety management system — put this in it.

That is why the vocabulary of annex 3.1 is the ordinary risk vocabulary — identify, analyse, assess, communicate; accept, avoid, transfer, mitigate — and why the goal in annex 3.2 is operational resilience rather than immunity. Nobody is claiming a ship can be made un-attackable.

blocks.h: IT versus OT - classify by function, not by box

blocks.p: Almost every candidate can say “IT is computers and OT is machinery”. The Guidelines distinguish them by what the data is for: information, versus control or monitoring of a physical process. That formulation is better because it classifies the awkward cases correctly:

ul: a loading computer is IT when it produces a stability report and OT when it drives valve and pump control — the same box, two classifications, depending on function;
an alarm and monitoring system is OT even though it controls nothing, because it monitors a physical process;
ECDIS is OT — it uses data to monitor and support control of navigation — and it is also connected for chart updating, which is exactly the convergence risk.

blocks.p: The follow-on point is the priority inversion: ashore, confidentiality usually leads; on the plant side, safety and availability lead. That is why office IT practice cannot simply be imported into the engine room — you cannot take main engine control offline for a monthly patch window, and a security control that risks availability may be worse than the threat it addresses.

blocks.h: Recommendatory guidance, mandatory duty

blocks.p: Three layers, and candidates routinely collapse them:

ol: MSC.428(98) — the obligation. Cyber risk must be appropriately addressed in the safety management system, by the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021.
MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 — the recommendatory guidance on how.
Industry and class material — the detail: the industry Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships, IACS recommendations, ISO/IEC 27001, NIST — to be used in the most current version.

blocks.p: So the honest answer to “is it mandatory?” is: the circular is not; the duty is. Verified at DOC and SMC audit, capable of a non-conformity, and capable of a port State control deficiency.

And at this sitting there is a fourth consideration worth a mark: IACS UR E26 and E27 apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024, so for newbuildings cyber resilience is a class requirement too.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Giving a number of functional elements without naming the edition. Five under Rev.2, six under Rev.3 with Govern first — and on this paper the day is unknowable, so name the revision.
Writing the elements as a sequence to be worked through once. They are expressly not sequential — concurrent and continuous, with feedback.
Treating the systems list as closed. The Guidelines say systems could include, but are not limited to.
Saying the Guidelines are mandatory. They are recommendatory; MSC.428(98) makes the subject mandatory through the ISM Code.
Confusing MSC.428(98) with the circular. The resolution is the obligation; the circular is the guidance.
Distinguishing IT from OT by hardware rather than by what the data is for.
Saying an air-gapped ship is out of scope. Removable media are the classic propagation route, and benign actions are within the definition.
Treating cyber risk as an attack-only problem. Corrupted, lost or compromised covers accident and failure too.
Saying the goal is to make the ship secure or immune. The stated goal is operational resilience.
Making it the ETO’s problem. Annex 3.3 puts the start at senior management level, and Rev.3’s Govern element makes accountability explicit.
Omitting the convergence point in limb (D), which is where the real risk lives — and missing that Rev.3 states segregation as a duty.
Letting limb (A) consume the answer. It is worth about four marks and the marks are in the naming.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: “How many elements of cyber risk management are there?” Name the revision. Five under Rev.2 of 7 June 2022; six under Rev.3 of 4 April 2025, Govern first. Anyone who tells you a single number without an edition is quoting one text and not knowing it.
“Are the elements sequential?” No — concurrent and continuous, incorporated in a risk-management framework, with effective feedback.
“Is the ECDIS IT or OT?” OT — it uses data to monitor and support control of a physical process, navigation. It is also connected for chart updating, which is the convergence risk in one example.

“Your ship has no internet. Do the Guidelines apply?” Yes. Unintended consequences of benign actions are in scope, and removable media are the classic route. An air-gapped ship is infected by memory stick.

“Who owns cyber risk on board?” It starts at senior management level (annex 3.3), and under Rev.3 the Govern element requires a person or entity accountable, with authority, support and expertise. It is not the ETO’s private problem.
“Which IMO instrument makes this mandatory?” None makes the Guidelines mandatory. MSC.428(98) makes cyber risk an ISM Code matter, by the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021.
“Can a port State control officer raise it?” Yes — as an ISM deficiency, since ISM compliance is inspectable.
“Is there a class requirement?” Yes, for newer tonnage — IACS UR E26 and E27, ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024.
“What is the primary technical control between IT and OT?” Network segregation — OT segmented from IT, protected from Internet-facing systems, with appropriate protection tools.

“Give the definition of maritime cyber risk.” A measure of the extent to which a technology asset could be threatened by a potential circumstance or event, which may result in operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which circular contains the Guidelines, and which revision applies? MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 - name the revision you are answering on, and note that Rev.3 is dated 4 April 2025.
Which committees approved it? The Maritime Safety Committee and the Facilitation Committee, jointly.
What did it supersede? The interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1526.
Name the functional elements. Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover - with Govern added and placed first under Rev.3.
Are they sequential? No - concurrent and continuous.

Name five vulnerable system categories. Bridge; cargo handling and management; propulsion, machinery management and power control; access control; communication systems - among others; the list is not closed.
Distinguish IT from OT. IT uses data as information; OT uses data to control or monitor a physical process.
Which resolution makes it mandatory, and by when? MSC.428(98) - the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021.
Which class requirements apply, and to which ships? IACS UR E26 and E27, to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024.
What is the goal of cyber risk management? Operational resilience, not immunity.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The whole question comes out of one document, so start by naming it — the circular and its revision. That single habit answers the hardest problem on this paper.
For limb (A), walk the ship from forward to aft and then ashore: BRIDGE → CARGO → MACHINERY → ACCESS → PASSENGER → PUBLIC → ADMIN → COMMS. Eight stops under Rev.2, restructured into nine under Rev.3.
For limb (B), two halves: the verbs — identify, analyse, assess, communicate; then accept, avoid, transfer, mitigate — and the elements: G-IPDRR, with G as the April 2025 addition.
For limb (D), one question decides every case: what is the data FOR? Information is IT; controlling or monitoring a physical process is OT.
And one sentence closes the answer: the guidance is recommendatory, the duty is not.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 — Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management. Approved jointly by MSC and FAL in 2017; superseded MSC.1/Circ.1526. Recommendatory.
Rev.2, 7 June 2022 — eight vulnerable-system categories at annex 2.1.1; five functional elements at annex 3.5; IT and OT described at annex 2.1.2.

Rev.3, 4 April 2025 — nine categories at annex 2.2.1; six functional elements with Govern first; formal IT and OT definitions at annex 2.1; segregation stated as a duty at annex 2.2.2; introduces Computer Based System (CBS).

Annex 1.1 — definition of maritime cyber risk. Annex 3.1 to 3.4 — the process, the resilience goal, the senior-management start, and current versus desired posture. Annex 3.6 and 3.7 — ongoing process with feedback; role-appropriate awareness.
Resolution MSC.428(98), 16 June 2017 — cyber risk to be addressed in the SMS in accordance with the ISM Code, by the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021.
ISM Code — element 1.2.2 (assess risks, establish safeguards), 7 (shipboard operations), 9 (non-conformities), 10 (maintenance), 12 (verification and review). Made mandatory by SOLAS chapter IX.
Resolution A.1185(33) — Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, the route by which an ISM deficiency is raised at the ship’s side.
IACS UR E26 and UR E27 — cyber resilience of ships, and of on-board systems and equipment; ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024.
External material the Guidelines point to: the industry Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships, IACS recommendations, ISO/IEC 27001, the NIST Framework — in their most current version.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, currency and an unusually candid evidence note

blocks.p: The circular this question is built on is not held by the corpus in any revision. A full-text search of the True Source corpus for MSC-FAL returns only the Cyber-Risk instrument log. What the corpus does hold, and what was read directly, is resolution MSC.428(98) — the resolution that makes the subject mandatory. So the mandatory layer of this answer is primary and the guidance layer is not.

The Rev.2 content reaches this answer through QP2403-Q5, the stem-identical March 2024 paper, which is the adjudicated donor and which sits thirteen months before this sitting — earlier, and therefore incapable of importing later law. The Rev.3 content reaches it through QP2510-Q5, a stem-identical paper from October 2025, which is six months after this sitting.

That post-sitting paper was not used as the donor. The recurrence tool preferred it, because it ranks by the size of the temporal gap and is blind to its sign; the playbook is explicit that a later solved donor does not transfer later law backwards, so reused_from is the March 2024 paper. But its Rev.3 material was re-verified rather than discarded, for one specific reason: the boundary it establishes opens inside this sitting month rather than after it. A 4 April 2025 revision is a live possibility for an April 2025 candidate in a way that an October 2025 development never could be.

The consequence is stated plainly: the 4 April 2025 date is the load-bearing fact of this question and it is not primary-sourced. It is INTERNAL_REUSE_VERIFIED, carries a currency-check flag, and the corpus should acquire both revisions as a priority. The answer’s construction does not fail if the date is wrong, because it names both editions and attributes every proposition to one of them.

No paragraph of either revision is quoted verbatim. The annex references given — 2.1, 2.1.1, 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 3.1 to 3.7 — are the structural locations recorded in the built MIW papers and should be re-verified when the circular is acquired. The exact wording of the nine Rev.3 categories and of the Rev.3 IT and OT definitions is not reproduced; both are given in substance.

IACS UR E26 and E27 are not held either — the corpus’s class folder holds notes only. Their application date is stated and no requirement of either is asserted. No industry guideline edition is dated, and no incident, vessel, company or attack statistic is named: none is held and all would be time-sensitive.

Currency. MSC.428(98) is the stable anchor — its DOC deadline is long past, so the ISM obligation is settled whichever revision of the Guidelines applies. IACS UR E26 and E27 are operative for ships contracted on or after 1 July 2024, nine months before this sitting. Nothing after April 2025 is asserted, the 34th Assembly of December 2025 is absent, and no content unique to the October 2025 regulatory position has been carried across.

questions.understand_first: This question looks like four unrelated tasks and is really one: it is checking whether you have read the circular it names. The systems list, the elements and the IT/OT distinction are all inside that one document, in its own terms. The idea worth taking away is that cyber risk was brought into shipping not as a new technical subject but as an extension of risk management the industry already does — which is exactly why a recommendatory circular sits alongside a resolution that puts the obligation inside the ISM Code. Nobody wrote a Cyber Code; they said you already have a safety management system, put this in it. On this paper there is one further thing, and it is unusual. The circular was revised on 4 April 2025 — inside this examination month — and the revision changes three of the four limbs. The source copy prints no examination day, so neither you nor anyone else can know which edition governed the candidate in the room. The professional answer to that is not to guess: it is to name the revision you are answering on, which is correct technique in any event and cannot be marked wrong either way.

steps.title: The instrument, its status, and the edition question
points: the stem names MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management
approved JOINTLY by the Facilitation Committee and the Maritime Safety Committee in 2017, superseding the interim guidelines in MSC.1/Circ.1526
maritime cyber risk - a measure of the extent to which a technology asset could be threatened by a potential circumstance or event
which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being CORRUPTED, LOST OR COMPROMISED
note the three verbs - it is not only about attack; accident and failure are in scope, and AVAILABILITY counts
THE GUIDELINES ARE EXPRESSLY RECOMMENDATORY - section 7 below explains why that does not make them optional
THE EDITION MATTERS ON THIS PAPER MORE THAN ON ANY OTHER
Rev.2 is dated 7 June 2022; Rev.3 is dated 4 APRIL 2025 - inside this examination month
Rev.3 changes three of the four printed limbs - the systems list, the number of functional elements, and the IT/OT treatment
NAME THE REVISION YOU ARE ANSWERING ON - that is correct technique and it cannot be marked wrong
Rev.3 also introduces the organising term Computer Based System (CBS), covering both IT and OT systems on board

steps.title: The on-board systems exposed to cyber risk
points: the Guidelines say vulnerable systems COULD INCLUDE, BUT ARE NOT LIMITED TO - this is a floor, not a closed list
the stem quotes the Guidelines' own reasoning - the vulnerabilities created by ACCESSING, INTERCONNECTING OR NETWORKING these systems create the risk
BRIDGE SYSTEMS - navigation, safety and communication systems: ECDIS, radar and ARPA, GNSS receivers, AIS, VDR, the integrated navigation system, the autopilot
CARGO HANDLING AND MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS - loading computer, ballast control, cargo control room, level and valve remote control, container reefer monitoring
PROPULSION, MACHINERY MANAGEMENT AND POWER CONTROL SYSTEMS - engine control room and bridge control, alarm and monitoring, power management, governor and PMS servers, remote vendor diagnostics
ACCESS CONTROL SYSTEMS - CCTV, bridge navigational watch alarm, ship security alert and shipboard security systems
PASSENGER SERVICING AND MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS - boarding, property management and passenger data systems
PASSENGER-FACING PUBLIC NETWORKS - guest wifi and entertainment, which are exposed by design
ADMINISTRATIVE AND CREW WELFARE SYSTEMS - ship administration, planned maintenance, purchasing, and crew internet and personal devices
COMMUNICATION SYSTEMS - satellite communications, VoIP, email and the shore link generally
under Rev.2 those are the EIGHT categories at annex 2.1.1; Rev.3 restructures the same ground into NINE at annex 2.2.1, rewriting the headings rather than simply appending one
so name the categories with a shipboard example each, and say which edition you are counting

steps.title: What cyber risk management means, and where it starts
points: THIS MATERIAL IS UNCHANGED BETWEEN THE EDITIONS, so it is the safe ground of limb (B) and comes first
annex 3.1 - cyber risk management is the process of IDENTIFYING, ANALYSING, ASSESSING AND COMMUNICATING a cyber-related risk
and then ACCEPTING, AVOIDING, TRANSFERRING OR MITIGATING it to an acceptable level
note that this is the ordinary risk-management vocabulary the industry already uses - that is the whole design idea
annex 3.2 - THE GOAL IS OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE, not immunity. Nobody claims a ship can be made un-attackable
annex 3.3 - effective cyber risk management SHOULD START AT SENIOR MANAGEMENT LEVEL, not with the ETO
annex 3.4 - compare the CURRENT cyber-risk posture with the DESIRED posture, and produce a PRIORITISED plan to close the gap
the controls are of three kinds - MANAGEMENT, PROCEDURAL AND TECHNICAL - and a purely technical answer is an incomplete one

steps.title: The functional elements - and how many there are
points: annex 3.5 sets out the functional elements, and states that they are NOT SEQUENTIAL - all should be concurrent and continuous
UNDER Rev.2, of 7 June 2022, there are FIVE - IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, RECOVER
UNDER Rev.3, of 4 April 2025, there are SIX - GOVERN is added and placed FIRST
GOVERN - designate a person or entity ACCOUNTABLE for planning, resourcing and executing cybersecurity activities, with the authority, support and expertise to do it
IDENTIFY - the systems, assets, data and capabilities which, if disrupted, pose risks to ship operations; know what you have before you defend it
PROTECT - risk control processes and measures, and contingency planning, to protect against a cyber event and ensure continuity
DETECT - activities to identify a cyber event in a timely manner
RESPOND - activities and plans to provide resilience and restore systems necessary for shipping operations or services impaired by a cyber event
RECOVER - measures to back up and restore cyber systems necessary for shipping operations impacted by a cyber event
annex 3.6 - together they constitute an ONGOING PROCESS WITH EFFECTIVE FEEDBACK MECHANISMS
annex 3.7 - awareness must be appropriate to each person's ROLE
so: five under Rev.2, six under Rev.3 with Govern first - name the edition and the answer stands either way
and whichever you give, DO NOT write them as a one-pass sequence - that is the commonest error on this limb

steps.title: Why cyber security matters in the maritime sector
points: argue it from the Guidelines' own reasoning, not from general cyber-security talk
THE RISK HAS MOVED OUT OF THE PHYSICAL DOMAIN - a ship can now be harmed without anyone being near it
A BRIDGE OR PROPULSION COMPROMISE IS A SAFETY EVENT, not an IT inconvenience - loss of steering, propulsion or position is a collision or grounding risk
IT-TO-OT PROPAGATION - the classic route is a chart update on a memory stick or a remote diagnostic session, and an air-gapped ship is infected by removable media
BENIGN ACTIONS COUNT - the definition covers information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised, so a mistaken software update is in scope as much as an attack
THE SHIP IS STRUCTURALLY HARD TO DEFEND - mixed vendor equipment of different ages, a small crew with no specialist, a thin and intermittent shore link, long asset lives
and equipment that cannot simply be patched, because a machinery control system cannot be rebooted mid-passage
TECHNICAL STANDARDS ALONE CANNOT KEEP UP - the threat changes faster than any standard can be amended, which is precisely why the response is risk management rather than a prescriptive rule
COMMERCIAL AND REGULATORY CONSEQUENCES - charterer and vetting expectations, insurance, port and terminal requirements, and the ISM consequence in section 7
THE SUPPLY CHAIN - third-party vendors, embedded systems and maintenance devices brought aboard are part of the ship's attack surface

steps.title: Information technology and operational technology
points: the Guidelines distinguish them by WHAT THE DATA IS FOR - not by the hardware
IT focuses on the USE OF DATA AS INFORMATION
OT focuses on the USE OF DATA TO CONTROL OR MONITOR PHYSICAL PROCESSES
Rev.3 promotes both to FORMAL DEFINITIONS at annex 2.1 and supplies worked examples, which the limb expressly asks for
IT EXAMPLES - ship administration and business systems, planned maintenance and purchasing, email, crew welfare and internet, personnel records, electronic manuals and certificates

OT EXAMPLES - engine and machinery control and alarm systems, power management, ballast and cargo control, ECDIS and the integrated navigation system, steering gear control, refrigeration and inert gas control
CLASSIFY BY FUNCTION, NOT BY BOX - a loading computer is IT when it produces a stability report and OT when it drives valve and pump control
and an alarm and monitoring system is OT even though it controls nothing, because it monitors a physical process
THE PRIORITY INVERSION - ashore, CONFIDENTIALITY usually leads; on the plant side, SAFETY AND AVAILABILITY lead
which is why office IT practice cannot simply be applied to the engine room - you cannot take the main engine control offline for a patch cycle
CONVERGENCE IS THE REAL RISK - the two are no longer separate, and under the Rev.3 vocabulary both are Computer Based Systems
a chart update on a memory stick, a remote vendor diagnostic session, or a loading computer reading from the business network all cross the boundary
so NETWORK SEGREGATION is the primary control - Rev.3 states it as a duty at annex 2.2.2: OT segmented from IT, protected from Internet-facing systems, and given appropriate protection tools

steps.title: How a recommendatory circular becomes a real obligation
points: THREE LAYERS, and keeping them apart is worth a mark
MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017, IS THE OBLIGATION - cyber risk must be appropriately addressed in the safety management system
the deadline was the FIRST ANNUAL VERIFICATION OF THE COMPANY'S DOCUMENT OF COMPLIANCE AFTER 1 JANUARY 2021 - long past at this sitting
MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 IS THE RECOMMENDATORY GUIDANCE on how to do it

INDUSTRY AND CLASS MATERIAL IS THE DETAIL - the industry Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships, IACS recommendations, ISO/IEC 27001 and the NIST Framework, named precisely because the Organization does not intend to write it
and the Guidelines require the MOST CURRENT VERSION of whatever is used
SO THE POSITION IS: the GUIDANCE on how to manage cyber risk is recommendatory, but WHETHER it is managed at all is an ISM Code matter
verified at Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate audit, and capable of being written up as a non-conformity
and capable of becoming a PORT STATE CONTROL DEFICIENCY under the Procedures for Port State Control, since ISM compliance is inspectable
A SECOND LAYER APPLIES AT THIS SITTING - IACS unified requirements UR E26 (cyber resilience of ships) and UR E27 (cyber resilience of on-board systems and equipment)
they apply to ships CONTRACTED FOR CONSTRUCTION ON OR AFTER 1 JULY 2024 - nine months before this examination
so for newer tonnage cyber resilience is a CLASS requirement and not only an SMS one, and mentioning it shows exactly the currency awareness this subject rewards
in practice on board: procedures under ISM element 7, maintenance under element 10, non-conformities under element 9, and company review under element 12

questions.memory_cue: One document answers all four limbs — so name the circular and its revision first (1). Then the four limbs are systems (2), meaning and elements (3, 4), why it matters (5), IT versus OT (6). And the mark most candidates miss is the closing one: recommendatory guidance, mandatory ISM duty (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management — approved jointly by MSC and FAL in 2017, superseding MSC.1/Circ.1526, and expressly recommendatory. NAME THE REVISION: Rev.2 of 7 June 2022 versus Rev.3 of 4 April 2025, which falls inside this sitting month. Maritime cyber risk = the extent to which a technology asset could be threatened, resulting in operational, safety or security failures from information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised — so accident counts, not just attack. (A) Vulnerable systems, “could include but are not limited to”: bridge; cargo handling and management; propulsion, machinery management and power control; access control; passenger servicing; passenger-facing public networks; administrative and crew welfare; communications — eight under Rev.2, restructured to nine under Rev.3. (B) Cyber risk management = identify, analyse, assess, communicate; then accept, avoid, transfer or mitigate. Goal is operational resilience, not immunity; starts at senior management; compare current with desired posture. Elements: IPDRR under Rev.2 (five); G-IPDRR under Rev.3 (six), Govern first — and they are NOT sequential. (C) Risk has left the physical domain; bridge or propulsion compromise is a safety event; IT-to-OT propagation by memory stick; benign actions count; the ship is hard to defend and cannot be patched freely; standards cannot keep up. (D) IT = data as information; OT = data to control or monitor a physical process — classify by function, not by box; OT prioritises safety and availability; convergence is the real risk and segregation is the primary control. The circular is recommendatory but MSC.428(98) makes cyber risk an ISM Code duty, by the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021 — and IACS UR E26/E27 apply to ships contracted on or after 1 July 2024.
keywords: could include but are not limited to
critical_numbers: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.2 is dated 7 June 2022; Rev.3 is dated 4 April 2025
Vulnerable system categories: eight under Rev.2, nine under Rev.3
Functional elements: five under Rev.2 (IPDRR), six under Rev.3 (Govern first)
MSC.428(98) adopted 16 June 2017
Cyber risk to be addressed in the SMS by the first annual DOC verification after 1 January 2021
IACS UR E26 and E27 apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024
The question prints a single (16) with four limbs and no printed limb split
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Resolution MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017, is what makes this subject mandatory: an approved safety management system should take account of cyber risk management in accordance with the objectives and functional requirements of the ISM Code, cyber risks being appropriately addressed in safety management systems no later than the first annual verification of the company's Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021. MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 itself — in whichever revision governs — is recommendatory guidance on how, not an obligation in its own right.
quick_revision.major_trap: Giving a number of functional elements without naming the edition. MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 is dated 4 April 2025 — inside this examination month — and it added a sixth element, GOVERN, placed first. Rev.2, in force until then, listed five: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. The source copy prints no examination day, so which edition governed cannot be known; the professional answer is to name the revision you are answering on, which cannot be marked wrong either way. The paired trap is treating the Guidelines as mandatory: they are expressly recommendatory, and it is MSC.428(98) that makes cyber risk an ISM Code duty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define maritime cyber risk as the Guidelines define it, and say why the wording matters.
retrieval_cards.answer: A measure of the extent to which a technology asset could be threatened by a potential circumstance or event, which may result in shipping-related operational, safety or security failures as a consequence of information or systems being CORRUPTED, LOST OR COMPROMISED. The three verbs matter: the subject is not only attack - accident, error and failure are in scope, and availability counts as much as confidentiality.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the definitional mark, and the three verbs are what stop the answer becoming a hacking essay.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many functional elements of cyber risk management are there?
retrieval_cards.answer: Name the revision. Under MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.2 of 7 June 2022 there are FIVE - Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Under Rev.3 of 4 April 2025 there are SIX, GOVERN having been added and placed first. Rev.3 falls inside an April 2025 sitting month, so state the edition you are answering on and the answer stands either way. In both editions the elements are expressly NOT sequential.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most likely error in either direction on this paper, and naming the edition is what makes the answer unmarkable-down.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the categories of on-board system the Guidelines identify as vulnerable.
retrieval_cards.answer: Bridge systems; cargo handling and management systems; propulsion, machinery management and power control systems; access control systems; passenger servicing and management systems; passenger-facing public networks; administrative and crew welfare systems; and communication systems. That is the Rev.2 set of eight; Rev.3 restructures the same ground into nine. The list is expressly not closed - systems 'could include, but are not limited to' these.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (A) is a naming exercise and the 'not limited to' qualification is itself a mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does cyber risk management mean, what is its goal, and where does it start?
retrieval_cards.answer: The process of identifying, analysing, assessing and communicating a cyber-related risk, and then accepting, avoiding, transferring or mitigating it to an acceptable level. The goal is OPERATIONAL RESILIENCE, not immunity. It should start at SENIOR MANAGEMENT LEVEL, and the approach compares the current cyber-risk posture with the desired posture and produces a prioritised plan. Controls are management, procedural and technical.
retrieval_cards.why: This material is identical in both revisions, so it is the safe ground of limb (B) and should be written first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish IT from OT, and classify a loading computer.
retrieval_cards.answer: IT focuses on the use of data AS INFORMATION; OT focuses on the use of data TO CONTROL OR MONITOR A PHYSICAL PROCESS. Classify by function, not by hardware: a loading computer is IT when it produces a stability report and OT when it drives valve and pump control. An alarm and monitoring system is OT even though it controls nothing, because it monitors a physical process.
retrieval_cards.why: The functional test is what classifies the awkward cases correctly, and the loading computer is the standard example.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship has no internet connection. Do the Guidelines apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes. Unintended consequences of benign actions are within the definition - information or systems being corrupted, lost or compromised - and removable media are the classic propagation route. An air-gapped ship is infected by memory stick: a chart update, a vendor's diagnostic laptop or a crew USB drive crosses from IT to OT.
retrieval_cards.why: It kills the assumption that cyber risk is only about internet-borne attack, and it is the clearest illustration of IT-to-OT propagation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which IMO instrument makes maritime cyber risk mandatory, and by when?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017. An approved safety management system should take account of cyber risk management in accordance with the objectives and functional requirements of the ISM Code, and cyber risks were to be appropriately addressed in safety management systems no later than the FIRST ANNUAL VERIFICATION OF THE COMPANY'S DOCUMENT OF COMPLIANCE AFTER 1 JANUARY 2021. The Guidelines themselves are recommendatory.
retrieval_cards.why: Three layers - obligation, guidance, detail - and collapsing them is the commonest architectural error in this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the priority inversion between IT and OT, and why does it matter on board?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ashore, confidentiality usually leads, then integrity, then availability. On the plant side, SAFETY AND AVAILABILITY lead - the process must keep running. That is why office IT practice cannot be imported wholesale into the engine room: you cannot take main engine control offline for a monthly patch window, and a security control that risks availability may be worse than the threat it addresses.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why OT cyber security is a distinct engineering problem rather than IT applied to machinery.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the primary control at the IT/OT boundary, and what is the underlying risk?
retrieval_cards.answer: Network segregation - OT systems segmented from IT systems, protected from Internet-facing systems, and provided with appropriate protection tools, which Rev.3 states as a duty at annex 2.2.2. The underlying risk is CONVERGENCE: the two domains are no longer separate, and under the Rev.3 vocabulary both are Computer Based Systems. A chart update on a memory stick, a remote vendor diagnostic session or a loading computer reading from the business network all cross the boundary.
retrieval_cards.why: Convergence is where the real risk lives, and it is the point limb (D) is actually testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is there a class requirement for cyber resilience at this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, for newer tonnage. IACS unified requirements UR E26 (cyber resilience of ships) and UR E27 (cyber resilience of on-board systems and equipment) apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024 - nine months before this examination. So for newbuildings cyber resilience is a class matter as well as an ISM one.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the currency point that shows awareness beyond the circular, and it dates cleanly before the sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the elements list not a sequence, and what happens if you write it as one?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Guidelines state expressly that the functional elements are not sequential - all should be concurrent and continuous and incorporated appropriately in a risk-management framework, constituting an ongoing process with effective feedback mechanisms. Writing them as a six-step process to be worked through once describes a project, not a management system, and misses the feedback that makes it work.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the commonest error on limb (B) and it is wrong under both revisions, so it costs marks whichever edition applies.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give four reasons why a ship is structurally hard to defend against cyber risk.
retrieval_cards.answer: Mixed vendor equipment of widely differing ages and standards; a small crew with no cyber specialist on board; a thin and intermittent shore link; asset lives measured in decades so equipment long outlives its software support; and control systems that cannot simply be patched, because a machinery control system cannot be rebooted mid-passage. Add the supply chain - vendors, embedded systems and maintenance devices brought aboard.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (C) is the only discursive limb, and these are the ship-specific reasons rather than general cyber-security commentary.
